docs.title: Response Parsing Example (JavaScript/TypeScript)
docs.text:
interface StatsCore {
    battery_mv: number;
    uptime_secs: number;
    errors: number;
    queue_len: number;
}

interface StatsRadio {
    noise_floor: number;
    last_rssi: number;
    last_snr: number;
    tx_air_secs: number;
    rx_air_secs: number;
}

interface StatsPackets {
    recv: number;
    sent: number;
    flood_tx: number;
    direct_tx: number;
    flood_rx: number;
    direct_rx: number;
    recv_errors?: number;  // present when frame is 30 bytes
}

function parseStatsCore(buffer: ArrayBuffer): StatsCore {
    const view = new DataView(buffer);
    const response_code = view.getUint8(0);
    const stats_type = view.getUint8(1);
    if (response_code !== 24 || stats_type !== 0) {
        throw new Error('Invalid response type');
    }
    return {
        battery_mv: view.getUint16(2, true),
        uptime_secs: view.getUint32(4, true),
        errors: view.getUint16(8, true),
        queue_len: view.getUint8(10)
    };
}

function parseStatsRadio(buffer: ArrayBuffer): StatsRadio {
    const view = new DataView(buffer);
    const response_code = view.getUint8(0);
    const stats_type = view.getUint8(1);
    if (response_code !== 24 || stats_type !== 1) {
        throw new Error('Invalid response type');
    }
    return {
        noise_floor: view.getInt16(2, true),
        last_rssi: view.getInt8(4),
        last_snr: view.getInt8(5) / 4.0,  // Unscale SNR
        tx_air_secs: view.getUint32(6, true),
        rx_air_secs: view.getUint32(10, true)
    };
}

function parseStatsPackets(buffer: ArrayBuffer): StatsPackets {
    const view = new DataView(buffer);
    if (buffer.byteLength < 26) {
        throw new Error('STATS_TYPE_PACKETS frame too short');
    }
    const response_code = view.getUint8(0);
    const stats_type = view.getUint8(1);
    if (response_code !== 24 || stats_type !== 2) {
        throw new Error('Invalid response type');
    }
    const result: StatsPackets = {
        recv: view.getUint32(2, true),
        sent: view.getUint32(6, true),
        flood_tx: view.getUint32(10, true),
        direct_tx: view.getUint32(14, true),
        flood_rx: view.getUint32(18, true),
        direct_rx: view.getUint32(22, true)
    };
    if (buffer.byteLength >= 30) {
        result.recv_errors = view.getUint32(26, true);
    }
    return result;
}

docs.title: Field Size Considerations
docs.text:
• Packet counters (uint32_t): May wrap after extended high-traffic operation.
  • Time fields (uint32_t): Max ~136 years.
  • SNR (int8_t, scaled by 4): Range -32 to +31.75 dB, 0.25 dB precision.

docs.title: Terminal Chat CLI
docs.text:
Below are the commands you can enter into the Terminal Chat clients:

set freq {frequency}

Set the LoRa frequency. Example: set freq 915.8

set tx {tx-power-dbm}

Sets LoRa transmit power in dBm.

set name {name}

Sets your advertisement name.

set lat {latitude}

Sets your advertisement map latitude. (decimal degrees)

set lon {longitude}

Sets your advertisement map longitude. (decimal degrees)

set af {air-time-factor}

Sets the transmit air-time-factor.

Note: set dutycycle is not available in Terminal Chat. Every other firmware — Repeater, Room Server, Sensor and Companion Radio — routes its set/get commands through the shared radio prefs handler and does support it (see CLI Commands). Terminal Chat is the sole exception: it has its own inline set handler covering only the six options listed above.

time {epoch-secs}

Set the device clock using UNIX epoch seconds. Example: time 1738242833

advert

Sends an advertisement packet

clock

Displays current time per device's clock.

ver

Shows the device version and firmware build date.

card

Displays your 'business card', for others to manually import

import {card}

Imports the given card to your contacts.

list {n}

List all contacts by most recent. (optional {n}, is the last n by advertisement date)

to

Shows the name of current recipient contact. (for subsequent 'send' commands)

to {name-prefix}

Sets the recipient to the first matching contact (in 'list') by the name prefix. (ie. you don't have to type whole name)

send {text}

Sends the text message (as DM) to current recipient.

reset path

Resets the path to current recipient, for new path discovery.

public {text}

Sends the text message to the built-in 'public' group channel

help

Lists the available commands.

docs.title: XIAO nRF52840 BME680 Sensor
docs.text:
Back to README

The Xiao_nrf52_bme680_sensor target creates a display-free MeshCore environmental sensor using a XIAO nRF52840, SX1262 and BME680. It measures once per minute, serves current telemetry on request and answers rate-limited !hillvue queries on Public and #hillvue, replying on the requesting channel.

The firmware is a leaf node. It receives traffic addressed to the sensor and listens for its Public-channel command, but it does not forward packets for other nodes.

docs.title: Guides
docs.text:
• Hardware and Wiring
  • Telemetry
  • Public-channel Commands
  • Access and Management
  • Building the Firmware

docs.title: Access and Management
docs.text:
Back to README

The sensor uses MeshCore's encrypted remote-management protocol and ACL. Live telemetry and management requests are handled separately from the unencrypted Public-channel !hillvue interface.

docs.title: Administrator access
docs.text:
The build default administrator password is password. Change it during first setup. A successful administrator login can configure the node, inspect status, request telemetry and manage ACL entries.

The first successful administrator-password login adds the companion identity to the ACL as an administrator. A known identity using a blank password retains its assigned ACL role. An unknown identity using a blank password, or a session using an incorrect password, receives read-only access with the app's limited guest interface.

Remote text/CLI commands require administrator permission. Telemetry requests are available to administrator and read-only guest sessions. Guest sessions cannot change settings or issue management commands.

docs.title: Persistent and temporary state
docs.text:
The following data persists across reboot:

  • Node identity and name.
  • Administrator password and administrator ACL entries.
  • Radio and advert configuration.

Sensor readings, air-quality calibration, command hashes, response-rate state and any pending second reply parts remain in RAM and reset at boot. Read-only guest sessions also remain in RAM; guest telemetry access does not write flash.

docs.title: Leaf-node policy
docs.text: Packet forwarding is hard-coded Off for this target. Remote attempts to enable repeat mode leave forwarding disabled, and status reports repeat mode as Off. This prevents the sensor from becoming a mesh repeater.

docs.title: Development and Testing
docs.text: Back to README

docs.title: Baseline
docs.text: The integration baseline is MeshCore v1.18.0, official release commit 81dbae592ffad40b4212bc0b37e82b38da08f4bc. Use the official companion-v1.18.0, repeater-v1.18.0 and room-server-v1.18.0 tags; all three resolve to this commit. Do not infer the baseline from unrelated fork-local version tags.

docs.title: Application modules
docs.text:
Module Responsibility main.cpp Hardware startup, serial console and main loop Bme680SensorMesh Binding to the upstream sensor runtime and radio callbacks SensorBotService Public commands, response formatting and asynchronous coordination PublicChannelSensorBot Command decoding, duplicate tracking and rolling rate limit PublicResponseQueue Bounded two-part replies and transmission-completion spacing RepeaterTraceProbe Path validation, timeouts, single retry and late-result fallback TraceTimingPolicy Hop/airtime timeout estimates and bounded queue, grace and report periods TraceRouteCandidates Three bounded passive alternatives and deterministic retry ranking TraceRouteHistory Four RAM-only, context-scoped recent route outcomes with lazy expiry TraceReportDelivery Frozen two-part report, bounded local retry and uncertain-outcome handling TraceDiagnostics Full directional SNR, passive progress and local outcome counters RepeaterNameCache Verified repeater names and bounded persistent cache Bme680Telemetry Cached measurements, channel discovery and telemetry encoding Bme680SensorManager Upstream BME680 driver adapter and installation altitude adjustment BME680AirQuality RAM-only calibration, warm-up count and relative score SensorManagementPolicy Read-only guest admission and administrator persistence

These modules live in examples/bme680_sensor/. They share one measurement snapshot. Public and management queries read that snapshot without sampling the BME680 or advancing its calibration. A failed sample retains the previous successful reading. Sensor readings and pending trace results do not persist.

docs.title: Baseline integration ledger
docs.text:
Baseline file Retained integration examples/simple_sensor/SensorMesh.h/.cpp Optional login, protocol-request, preference and persistence hooks; default policies retain the standard sensor behaviour src/Dispatcher.h/.cpp Generic transmit-start callback and queued-packet inspection/cancellation src/Mesh.cpp TRACE header and complete-path bounds checks src/helpers/TracePathBounds.h Small shared TRACE validation helper src/helpers/ClientACL.h/.cpp Optional administrator-preserving client allocation, sharing the standard allocator variants/xiao_nrf52/target.h/.cpp Selectable sensor-manager type, defaulting to the upstream environment manager

The standard examples/simple_sensor/main.cpp and src/helpers/sensors/EnvironmentSensorManager.cpp match the baseline. Earlier humidity-decoding and request-length corrections, together with request-scope-aware login/telemetry replies, remain generic sensor corrections. Later upstream imports are distinct from this application and are retained.

The core does not include custom bot, air-quality or guest-policy classes. The XIAO custom environment selects the application; there is no bot flag controlling unrelated authentication or storage behaviour.

docs.title: Automated validation
docs.text:
pio test -e native -e native_sensor -e native_kiss_modem
bash bin/check-sensor-boundaries.sh
pio run -e Xiao_nrf52_bme680_sensor -e Xiao_nrf52_sensor_baseline
pio run -e Xiao_nrf52_repeater -e Xiao_nrf52_room_server -e Xiao_nrf52_companion_radio_usb

The original native suite covers command parsing, rate-limit boundaries, reply splitting, trace state transitions and malformed TRACE paths. The native_sensor suite uses actual MeshCore encryption, signatures, packet handling, dispatcher queues, telemetry encoding and ACL storage. Its simulated clock, radio and filesystem make failure timing and write counts repeatable. Hardware randomness is replaced only by deterministic test input. The legacy exact-time packet cases explicitly suppress settling; production defaults and separate settling tests enable it. Multi-node tests use the production default.

Integration cases include silent retry, duplicate command reception, cancelling a queued retry, late first-result fallback, multipart spacing after actual TX completion, verified repeater names, and radio recovery after an advert TX timeout. Storage tests cover capacity, ambiguous hashes, corrupt cache data, failed file replacement and avoiding writes for unchanged adverts.

Channel tests cover interleaved Public and #hillvue requests, multipart reply ownership, busy notices, trace results and late-result fallback. Pending parts and active traces retain a bounded channel index rather than a mutable global reply destination. Rate limiting is shared; duplicate tracking includes the source channel. Candidate lookup also handles matching one-byte channel hashes.

Trace expiry now schedules the next action rather than invalidating an otherwise matching result. Both transmitted attempt records remain live through final grace and unsent failure reporting. The radio adapter commits failure at TX start; queued failures and retries are cancelled before their pool handles are discarded. Monotonic, randomly seeded tags distinguish successive attempts.

The multi-repeater suite uses real MeshCore forwarding and encryption with simulated airtime, directed links, delay and packet loss. It covers two/three repeaters, two-byte hashes, same-route retry, alternate-route retry, asymmetric links and useful late results. The medium is not a physical RF or collision model.

An additional AddressSanitizer run checks the real-crypto suites:

ASAN_OPTIONS=detect_leaks=0 pio test -e native_sensor_asan

Leak detection is disabled because the baseline static packet-pool test objects do not implement destruction. Tests separately require all packet slots to be returned after each completed scenario. Address/buffer checks remain enabled.

Initial command, air-quality, cache, ACL and real-crypto tests were run against the implementation before extraction. The extraction also corrects two behavioural defects: non-finite sensor inputs cannot advance calibration, and remote telemetry requests now use the same cached readings as Public commands.

The compile-only baseline environment exercises ordinary BME680 telemetry without any custom sensor-manager or altitude-offset definition. This also guards against the previous misplaced altitude-offset fallback macro.

docs.title: Implementation validation
docs.text:
Recorded on 19 October 2026:

Check Result Pre-extraction characterization tests Passed before moving application code native 88 test cases passed native_sensor 108 test cases passed, including 49 packet integration and 21 network-medium cases native_kiss_modem 8 test cases passed native_sensor_asan The same 108 sensor cases passed with AddressSanitizer Custom sensor, baseline sensor, companion USB, repeater and room-server builds All five passed Baseline boundary check and git diff --check Passed Strict MkDocs site build Passed Named UF2 generation and DFU ZIP integrity Passed Physical sensor, phone app, RF and OTA acceptance Pending: no attached hardware

The native companion-preferences suite is conditionally excluded by its existing platform guard; it does not exercise this sensor application. No test case in the executed suites failed.

The initial extracted sensor build reports 31,200 bytes of static RAM and 353,196 bytes of flash, compared with 31,168 and 354,604 before extraction. These are linker figures, not measured peak heap or stack usage. The new Cayenne buffers are allocated once at startup, not for each telemetry request.

The completed trace remediation reports 31,440 bytes of static RAM and 355,724 bytes of flash, compared with 31,232 and 353,692 before this remediation. The additional trace state therefore costs 208 bytes of static RAM and 2,032 bytes of flash. It adds no heap buffers or flash writes. Local sanitizer validation used a signature-verified Fedora runtime extracted under /tmp, without installing system packages.

docs.title: Trace plan completion
docs.text:
• The two deadline-boundary regressions failed before the implementation changed.
  • Per-attempt result validation, final grace, cancellable failure reports and bounded queue ownership are implemented and tested.
  • Airtime estimation, a single passive alternate route and original-route fallback rendering are implemented and tested.
  • Limits, channel ownership, formatting, packet-pool return and zero-write behaviour are covered by regression and multi-repeater tests.
  • CI runs the regular tests, sanitizer tests and five firmware targets.
  • Firmware artifacts and documentation are validated separately from hardware.

The software extraction and earlier remediation are complete. Physical RF, phone-app presentation and OTA installation remain pending acceptance on an attached node; simulation is not a substitute for those checks.

The software extraction, automated checks and build integration are complete. Full hardware acceptance is not claimed until the following checklist passes.

docs.title: Trace reliability validation
docs.text:
The pre-change baseline passed 162 regular cases. The reliability change adds retained report delivery, bounded allocation/queue recovery, conservative radio start handling, a first-probe settling window, recent route evidence and passive diagnostics. All buffers are fixed-capacity; history and progress are RAM-only. Idle operation performs no route scans or periodic radio/configuration queries.

Reliability plan item Software validation Retain successful results through report delivery Allocation/queue recovery, frozen text, multipart gap, expiry and uncertain-outcome cases pass Recover from local probe failures Admission backoff, rejected starts, remaining-attempt budget and late-first recovery pass Airtime-aware first-probe settling Production defaults, quiet extension, hard limit, unrelated traffic and RTT exclusion pass Rank alternatives and retain recent evidence Three-candidate/four-history bounds, channel/radio context, expiry and deterministic ranking pass Directional SNR and passive progress Both hash widths and one through ten repeaters pass; malformed/stale progress is rejected Collision/contention/hash-collision tests 21 deterministic network cases pass, including eight seeded-loss runs Physical RF measurements and OTA install Pending: no attached XIAO; no physical performance claim

Final automated validation comprises 204 regular cases and 108 repeated sensor cases under AddressSanitizer: 312 executions passed. The existing sanitizer leak-detection qualification above still applies; packet-pool return is checked explicitly by integration/network tests.

The final custom sensor linker reports 32,408 bytes of static RAM and 362,956 bytes of flash. Static RAM increased by 968 bytes from the preceding 31,440-byte build, below the two-KiB review budget. These figures exclude the linker's reserved heap area and do not claim a measured runtime stack/heap peak. The additional modules introduce no per-request application heap allocations or new persistent formats/writes.

The radio medium now has optional half-duplex, overlapping-frame collision, hidden-terminal, six-decibel capture-threshold, busy-channel and seeded-loss models. It includes standard direct-forwarding delay estimates and competing repeaters sharing a one-byte prefix. These are reproducible approximations, not measured RF capture behaviour. Packet ownership callbacks are synchronous and precede dispatcher release; reports retain no packet handle after callback completion. No asynchronous callback may refer to a recycled allocation. The adapter runs queued-work expiry before the dispatcher, preventing an old queued report from starting after its deadline when the loop resumes late.

Production conservatively treats rejected report starts as uncertain: the RadioLib Boolean interface does not expose whether an error occurred before or after the TX command. Tests explicitly mark a simulated rejection as definitely unsent only when their fake radio emits no frame. No generic MeshCore callback or forwarding changes were needed for this reliability change.

Hardware acceptance remains a separate gate. Use an isolated/controlled RF setup: #hillvue alone does not isolate interference on the shared frequency. For each important condition, compare baseline and updated firmware, preferably interleaving at least thirty runs each where practical. Observe the existing command limit and allow each operation to finish. Record firmware, radio settings, topology, trial count, confirmed starts, potentially emitting probe submissions, local failures, timeouts, selected route, passive progress, RTT, total response delay, local report outcome, companion receipt, duplicates and airtime. Include clean two-/three-relay routes, slow settings, contention, asymmetry, alternate paths, delayed results and multipart reception. Report sample sizes and uncertainty rather than claiming a universal success rate.

docs.title: Storage and firmware updates
docs.text:
The /repeaters, /s_contacts, identity and preference formats are unchanged. Module relocation requires no erase or settings migration. Administrator state and repeater names retain their existing write policies. Service buffers are bounded; normal request processing does not allocate new application objects.

The custom target keeps the established Xiao_nrf52_bme680_sensor.uf2 and Xiao_nrf52_bme680_sensor.zip artifact names.

docs.title: Trace scope regression coverage
docs.text:
The scope adapter is shared between the production sensor and native test runtime. Native tests use real RegionMap resolution, transport-key HMACs, MeshCore encryption, Dispatcher and packet pools. Each delayed reply owns its channel, scope key and path-hash width. Scope selection helpers also serve the upstream synchronous sensor reply path; the baseline firmware build checks that this generic API remains compatible.

test_sensor_dispatcher isolates actual TX-start timing, scheduled and busy-channel waiting, failed-start ownership, selective cancellation and ordinary consumer completion. test_sensor_scope covers both watched channels, interleaved multipart messages, busy notices, trace retry/fallback, allocation and queue recovery, scope removal and key rotation. Route tests isolate history by the complete scope key and prevent foreign-scope command copies extending settling. Network tests validate transport codes on relays that reject unscoped floods, including wrong-scope controls, multipart delivery and trace failure reports.

These tests run in the regular and sanitizer sensor environments. Firmware resource measurements, validation commands and separate physical acceptance status are recorded in the scope implementation validation report.

docs.title: Average bidirectional trace SNR
docs.text:
Trace reports display one node per outward link, beginning at the sensor. For zero-based repeater index i and N repeaters, the paired samples are i and 2*N - 1 - i. Raw signed quarter-dB readings remain available in diagnostics; their promoted signed sum divided by eight yields the average in dB. The final sample is the sensor's receive SNR. Rounding happens only when rendering one decimal place. The header explicitly says avg SNR.

test_sensor_trace_snr covers every route length from one to ten and both hash widths, signed extrema, opposite signs, eighth-dB precision, node order, multipart output, retry precedence and original-route fallback. A packet-medium case assigns different SNR values to each directed link and exercises actual MeshCore forwarding for both widths, including sensor RX and exclusion of the requester link. Existing scoped delivery tests continue to cover channel/scope retention. See the average SNR validation report.

Physical acceptance must compare the paired raw readings and displayed averages on a controlled asymmetric link. Packet-medium tests validate protocol ordering and arithmetic but cannot establish real radio measurements.

docs.title: Destination trace discovery
docs.text:
test_sensor_target_trace tests the public-key-prefix command through real MeshCore encryption, authenticated PATH decoding, the shared production peer binding and Dispatcher. It covers unknown/ambiguous/malformed prefixes, all one-to-ten-repeater routes at both hash widths, RTC tags, bounded discovery retries, radio-start/queue/allocation failure, cancellation before radio send, scoped replies, late old-target replies, retry/fallback SNRs and full-target history isolation. Transient discovery peers are not added to the sensor ACL. Management PATH ownership and other authenticated admin traffic are exercised against the native ACL runtime.

The packet-medium tests include a known-client/replay-protected repeater responder: targeted discovery and the complete loop cross real forwarding nodes, both channels, both hash widths and relays rejecting unscoped floods. Unknown remote clients time out without automatic login or ACL changes. The sensor's peer binding consumes RESPONSE/PATH packets without applying them to management routes; ordinary management PATHs retain their existing callback. A generic Mesh PATH decoder guard rejects a path that does not fit in the authenticated decrypted payload before reading its extra fields; an encrypted truncated-path regression covers this under ASan.

See the destination trace validation record for the commands, measured resource changes and separate physical acceptance.

docs.title: Trace request acknowledgement and overall deadline
docs.text:
TraceTransactionBudget defines a fixed 60,000 ms transaction and a 5,000 ms terminal-report reserve. Acceptance freezes the deadline and acknowledgement text at 60 seconds. At 55 seconds, unfinished discovery/probing becomes a stage-specific failure report; at 60 seconds, cleanup releases trace ownership. Timers use wrap-safe monotonic millisecond comparisons.

Discovery and probe windows are clamped at actual TX start using cached airtime policy and live remaining work time. First/retry probes divide that time by two/one. Initial/final discovery use six-second stage leases within a 40-second control cutoff. Guest login permits three attempts total (two retries), each with a fresh durable request timestamp. It has separate eight-second queue and post-TX-completion reply leases, with an airtime-based watchdog between them. Every lease remains clipped to the same control cutoff; delayed/duplicate completion cannot rearm an expired or cancelled operation. This leaves opportunities for the later stages without requiring the old maximum ten-hop windows to fit. Admissions check estimated TX watchdog plus scheduled delay against remaining work time. No retry or response restarts either deadline. TX-start observers do only timer arithmetic and never query the radio.

TraceRequestAcknowledgement owns a single immutable message independently of TraceReportDelivery. Its admission lease is ten seconds, followed by a cached actual-packet TX watchdog, bounded by the maximum-frame allowance, if transmission starts. Only definitely unsent failures can retry. The acknowledgement prelude suspends discovery and probe queue clocks; a failure to acknowledge does not fail the trace. Queued expiry is checked before Dispatcher polling; TX observer expiry is checked after completion callbacks have had their normal opportunity. Deadline cleanup never frees a Dispatcher-owned in-flight allocation. Ordinary public reply processing continues during the acknowledgement stage.

test_sensor_trace_ack covers fixed deadlines, report reservation and budget sharing, all route lengths and both hash widths, rollover and exact deadline boundaries, real Dispatcher acknowledgement ordering and failure recovery, slow TX, allocation pressure, cancellation, status, duplicates, targeted discovery, and both channels/widths/scopes. Older exact-phase integration tests explicitly complete acknowledgement through a transport seam to retain their probe/report timing characterization. The dedicated acknowledgement suite and network simulation leave that seam disabled and run real Dispatcher transmission. Network tests separately capture acknowledgements and terminal reports; the added flood can cause contention and consume the second allowed probe attempt.

See the 60-second cap validation record. The earlier acknowledgement plan and initial validation record the superseded conservative timeout policy.

docs.title: Named destination acknowledgement
docs.text:
The destination overload of RepeaterNameCache::resolvePrefix returns a copied full key and full display label from the same uniquely matching entry. It clears both outputs for unknown/ambiguous prefixes. It preserves words such as Repeater, unlike the compact hop-label formatter, and normalizes whitespace without altering persisted names or the cache schema. Unusable names use the lowercase two-byte prefix as a label; they never replace the full protocol key.

TraceRequestAcknowledgement::begin optionally formats Trace requested to Y. The complete message is copied at acceptance. Its existing buffer size is unchanged; bounded destination-only UTF-8 truncation keeps the fixed timeout suffix. Tests cover exact fit, overflow, invalid UTF-8/fallback, mutable input, queue retry/cache rename/eviction, full-key authenticated discovery, both public channels and scoped network replies. Bare acknowledgement, compact hop names and the 60-second cap remain unchanged.

See the implementation plan and validation record.

docs.title: First contact, durable timestamps and advert-route fallback
docs.text:
TraceDiscovery now owns the initial request, public guest login, final request and passive advert wait as separate bounded phases, with one control-packet owner. This folds the planned first-contact/login components into the existing controller to avoid competing owners. Login uses the stock 1.18 response shape and server timestamp; only a fresh-tag ordinary PATH supplies an authenticated route. A delayed login is advisory and cannot commit a route or change clocks.

TraceRequestClock reserves 256 values in two independently committed, identity-bound CRC records and verifies both before issuing a timestamp. Reboot starts beyond the highest surviving reserved bound. Faults fail closed for authenticated requests; advert fallback remains possible. No journal/cache I/O occurs in RX/TX observers. TraceGuestPolicy persists public/off independently of upstream NodePrefs and fails closed on a corrupt existing policy record.

TraceAdvertRouteCache stores compact verified-advert route hints in less than 10 KiB, with 48 full-key entries and two alternatives each. It reverses outgoing intermediates, appends the target and constructs the return loop. Observations are scope/profile/width-bound, known-age hints expire at 24 hours, and restored unknown-age hints are explicitly probationary. Atomic sidecar replacement with backup recovery coalesces changes for 30 seconds and throttles routine saves to ten minutes. Disk records contain only populated entries and replacement keeps at most two route files, important for the XIAO's 28 KiB internal filesystem. Stored hints/outcomes never replace a fresh round-trip result.

The scope binding captures outgoing default scope separately from public reply context, and dispatches owned login PATH/RESPONSE without installing management routes. Authenticated current-tag replies can return on a different scope, matching Zen's eligibility; mismatches are counted. TX observers use cached budgets and record control timing. Discovery diagnostics retain stage counters, clock health, peer clock regression, role, rejection and route provenance.

The stock repeater login/replay helpers were extracted into generic RepeaterLogin.h and are used by both production and the native network target. The runtime sensor adds only a protected default-scope value accessor, while the RTC adapter exposes hardware-clock presence. No custom bot policy enters core Mesh/Dispatcher. Tests no longer seed an ACL for the essential first-contact success case and cover protected guest and persisted login-free fallback.

See the repair plan and implementation validation.

docs.title: Trace lifecycle recovery review
docs.text:
Recovery regressions now attempt another trace after success, discovery timeout, queue exhaustion, rejected radio start, probe timeout and queued-report expiry. The targeted suite also injects a lost report completion notification, a new command arriving exactly as discovery expires, cancellation during queue/wait/ report phases, late cancelled replies, delayed TX completion polling, and the realistic 1,512 ms maximum-frame airtime estimate at the shipped radio defaults. The parser tests cover cancellation with an exhausted normal command budget. Report unit tests cover stale loop timestamps and a wrap-safe missing-callback watchdog. These are selected by the existing regular and ASan environments.

The complete review and validation record distinguishes the expected thirty-second discovery wait from reproduced lifecycle defects and records firmware artifacts and physical acceptance limits.

docs.title: Hardware acceptance
docs.text:
Automated tests cannot establish RF delivery, physical sensor accuracy or the phone app's presentation. Complete these checks on the installed XIAO before marking hardware acceptance passed:

  1. Install the named UF2 and confirm identity, radio settings and administrator access survive the update.
  2. Observe the first reading, ten-sample warm-up and continued one-minute sampling; issue repeated telemetry queries and confirm warm-up does not advance between samples.
  3. Check blank-password and incorrect-password guest telemetry in the official app and Zen companion; confirm management controls remain restricted.
  4. Check administrator status, owner info, configuration and ACL management.
  5. Exercise !hillvue, combined measurements, voltage, ping, path and trace, respecting the rolling four-command limit.
  6. Test real two- and three-repeater routes on both watched channels, retry success, an observed alternate route, late fallback and multipart delivery during ordinary network traffic. Repeat with a slower radio configuration; compare observed RTT with the airtime-aware deadline. Confirm a valid late result replaces an unsent failure, with no contradictory terminal report.
  7. Trigger remote Advert and verify whether the advert is heard, its command confirmation arrives, and subsequent telemetry/Public commands still work. The reported app Advert timeout is not reproduced by the simulated radio recovery test and remains a hardware acceptance item.
  8. Install the named DFU ZIP through the intended OTA application and repeat the basic access and telemetry checks.

No XIAO serial device was attached during this implementation. Hardware and phone-app acceptance must therefore be recorded separately from automated test/build results. Zen version and OLED/E-ink build instructions apply to the Zen application; those sources/environments are absent on this sensor branch.

docs.title: Trace request-clock recovery
docs.text:
The durable request floor is separate from calendar time. Use existing local or trusted administrator clock, clock sync, or time <epoch-seconds> commands to inspect/synchronize the actual RTC when needed; only move it forward from a trusted source. A valid journal still prevents issued values from being reused if the RTC restarts behind that floor. Inspect diagnostics().clock_healthy and control tags to distinguish local journal failure from an unexplained remote silence. A missing login/response is not proof of replay rejection.

One surviving valid replica is recovered on begin. After a transient filesystem failure, repair available storage and reboot so the allocator reloads its safe bounds. If both records are damaged, retain advert fallback and restore a known safe journal pair through local maintenance before re-enabling authenticated requests. Do not delete both records or invent a timestamp to bypass remote replay checks. Without a safe backup or a demonstrably higher trusted bound, explicit operator recovery/re-provisioning is needed. No destructive journal reset or remote ACL reset is performed automatically.

docs.title: Hardware and Wiring
docs.text:
Back to README

The firmware target is built for a Seeed Studio XIAO nRF52840, an SX1262 LoRa module and one BME680 I2C sensor. There is no display or local user interface.

docs.title: BME680
docs.text:
BME680 XIAO nRF52840 Purpose VIN/3V3 3V3 3.3 V supply GND GND Common ground SCL D6 I2C clock SDA D7 I2C data

The firmware expects I2C address 0x76. Configure a breakout that defaults to 0x77 for 0x76 before use. Keep all signal levels at 3.3 V.

D6 and D7 are intentional. The radio uses D4 and D5, so the default XIAO I2C pin pair is unavailable to the BME680.

docs.title: SX1262 radio
docs.text:
SX1262 signal XIAO pin DIO1 D1 RESET D2 BUSY D3 NSS/CS D4 RXEN D5 SCK D8 MISO D9 MOSI D10

The target uses SX1262 DIO2 for RF switching and DIO3 for a 1.8 V TCXO. TXEN is not assigned to a separate XIAO pin. Confirm that these assumptions match the radio module before applying power.

The firmware permits a configured TX power up to 22 dBm. Use an antenna suitable for the selected frequency and configure radio parameters that are legal for the installation location.

docs.title: Power and indicators
docs.text:
The node can run continuously from USB power. The XIAO's red LED is used as the LoRa transmit indicator and briefly illuminates when the radio sends.

Supply voltage is included in telemetry. The standard XIAO nRF52840 battery measurement and low-voltage protection remain active when a battery is fitted.

docs.title: Public-channel Commands
docs.text:
Back to README

The node listens on MeshCore's built-in Public channel and #hillvue for messages beginning with the exact command word !hillvue. Matching is case-insensitive. Each response stays on the requesting channel, including delayed message parts, trace results, fallback results and error notices. Both channels share the same four-command-per-minute limit and active trace.

Replies retain the request's transport scope through delayed and multipart messages, trace results, fallback results and error notices. A recognised scope is mirrored; an explicitly unscoped request receives an unscoped reply. If a transport scope cannot be resolved, the sensor uses its configured default scope, or replies unscoped if no usable default exists. The selection is captured when the command is accepted, so later traffic or default-scope changes do not redirect a pending reply. A busy notice follows the new request's scope while the running trace keeps its original scope.

Hashtag channels are not private: anyone who knows the name can derive the key.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
Message Response !hillvue All measurements !hillvue all All measurements !hillvue t Temperature !hillvue h Humidity !hillvue p Pressure !hillvue a Air quality !hillvue v XIAO battery voltage !hillvue ping Pong reachability reply !hillvue path Repeater path taken by this request !hillvue trace Incoming command route RTT and average bidirectional link SNR !hillvue trace 4df5 Discover and trace to the known repeater with public-key prefix 4df5 !hillvue trace status Current discovery/probe/report phase, attempt and receive/queue time remaining !hillvue trace cancel Stop the active trace and cancel its queued work

An option is selected by its first letter, so forms such as temp, Temperature and T all select temperature. Likewise, v, volt and voltage select voltage. Multiple space-separated options can be combined:

!hillvue t air
!hillvue Temperature Humidity
!hillvue p h a
!hillvue voltage t

!hillvue ping is standalone and cannot be combined with measurements. It uses the same traffic limits as other commands and does not require sensor data. Pong confirms that the node received the command, but does not measure mesh round-trip time in milliseconds.

!hillvue path is also standalone. It reports the repeaters traversed by the request on its way to the sensor, using names from verified repeater adverts where available. Unknown or ambiguous names are shown as path hashes. This is the first received route, not necessarily the best route or the return path. The sensor retains up to 48 repeater names in its internal flash filesystem; unchanged adverts do not cause writes. The reply appears on the requesting channel, not as a private message to the requester. Long paths use at most two messages, labelled 1/2 and 2/2, with a three-second gap after the first transmission completes. Replies split between repeaters, preserving their order and using the same short names as trace replies. Paths that exceed both messages end with ...truncated. Short paths remain one message; the shared four-requests-per-minute limit is unchanged.

Path and trace display names omit the whole words repeater and rptr, ignoring case, before applying the existing 12-byte UTF-8-safe name limit. For example, Hillvue Repeater becomes Hillvue, and Tamworth rptr becomes Tamworth. Whitespace is tidied; stored advert names are unchanged. If removal leaves an empty name, the repeater's path hash is displayed instead.

!hillvue trace without a destination sends one direct MeshCore trace out through the repeaters in the received request path and back to itself, then reports the elapsed milliseconds as a round-trip measurement and the average of both directional SNR readings for each link. Nodes are listed once, starting with the nearest repeater to the sensor and proceeding towards the requester. Each node's displayed SNR describes its link to the preceding node (the sensor for the first entry). For example:

Trace: 1540 ms RTT (avg SNR)
1 Ridge -4.0 dB
2 Valley +1.0 dB

For the first entry, sensor-to-repeater -6 dB and repeater-to-sensor -2 dB produce -4.0 dB. This is the arithmetic mean of the two dB readings from the selected trace attempt, not an average over time. Values are averaged before rounding to one decimal place. Retry and late fallback reports use their own route's samples; the first link includes the sensor's final received SNR. An average can hide a weaker direction, so it is not a weakest-link score. The final repeater-to-requester link is outside the trace measurement.

To choose a destination instead of using the command's incoming route, send !hillvue trace 4df5. The four hexadecimal characters select the first two bytes of a full public key in the sensor's verified repeater-advert cache (up to 48 named repeaters, including persisted adverts). Uppercase hexadecimal is accepted. The sensor must already know the full identity; four characters alone cannot identify an unknown node. An absent prefix reports Trace: unknown repeater 4df5; multiple cached matches report Trace: ambiguous repeater 4df5. Neither case starts discovery. Malformed prefixes or combined trace/measurement commands are ignored. Both trace forms are standalone commands.

For a selected destination, the sensor first tries standard authenticated path discovery. If the repeater does not yet recognise the sensor, the default public first-contact policy makes an anonymous login with the empty public guest credential, allowing two retries (three transmissions total), then sends a fresh authenticated request. No administrator password is needed or guessed. A target with protected guest access may ignore that login; lack of a reply does not establish that the repeater is unreachable. Private/local administration can select get trace.login or set trace.login public|off. A successful login may create a transient client entry on the target. An unexpected administrator grant is not used by this workflow; tracing falls back instead.

If discovery cannot obtain a path, the stationary sensor can use a reversed route from that repeater's previously verified flooded adverts. It retains up to two candidate routes for each of 48 identities in a separate persisted cache. Known-age hints expire after 24 hours. Restored hints without reliable calendar age are probationary candidates, never freshly discovered routes. Every attempt sends a new round-trip TRACE: old RTT/SNR/results are never returned as current. If one route fails, a distinct alternate may use the one remaining probe. Advert fallback can succeed with no login and no target ACL entry. On first installation, the route cache is empty even if old stored names are present: allow the sensor to receive genuine flooded adverts before relying on fallback. After collection and a deferred save, those hints can survive reboot.

The selected repeater remains the final outward entry, including a direct neighbour. Final output and average-SNR rules match bare trace. Ten repeaters includes the target; one/two-byte hashes are supported. Unsupported paths are never probed. An advert authenticates the originating identity/data, not its mutable flood path or reverse reachability, so a candidate can still fail if links are asymmetric or topology changes. Ambiguous short-hash labels remain ambiguous.

Control traffic stops at 40 seconds from command acceptance, leaving time for route probing. Initial and final discovery each have a six-second stage lease, including queueing, transmission and reply waiting. Guest login instead has an eight-second queue allowance, an airtime-based transmission watchdog, then up to eight seconds for its reply starting at successful local TX completion. Queueing and airtime do not consume that reply window. Each phase is clipped to the original 40-second control cutoff; a login completing close to that cutoff has less than eight seconds left. Failed or expired transmissions never start a reply window. The 55-second work and 60-second overall limits below always apply. trace status identifies guest login, waiting for adverts or advert-route probing, and shows remaining overall seconds. Timing changes never extend the original promise.

The target must recognise the sensor's identity to answer authenticated discovery; a phone's or Zen's earlier login does not register the sensor. Authenticated discovery replies are matched by full identity, MAC and fresh request tag even if a target's return scope differs; the difference is recorded. Outgoing control uses the configured default transport scope (otherwise the resolved command scope or unscoped), and the local configured discovery hash width. Public replies retain the original command's captured context. Cached advert hints must match the selected control scope and radio configuration.

Durable request timestamps prevent ordinary reboot/clock rollback from reusing already issued trace login/discovery timestamps. Storage/clock failure disables further authenticated requests and still permits advert fallback. Failures such as Trace: guest login not acknowledged, Trace: request clock unavailable, radio busy, transmit failed or discovery timed out describe the known stage; they do not prove RF unreachability or permission denial from silence alone.

Use !hillvue trace cancel to stop waiting without rebooting. Cancellation acts on the sensor's shared trace from either watched channel. It removes queued discovery, probe and report packets and prevents further retries/parts. A packet already on air cannot be recalled and remains owned by Dispatcher; its late callbacks/results cannot restart the cancelled operation. The cancel reply uses the operator's requesting channel and scope. The normal four-command-per-minute limit still applies to starts and status requests. Cancelling an active trace is allowed even when those slots are exhausted, with one acknowledgement for the cancelled operation; idle cancel requests use the normal limit.

Every accepted bare or destination trace first schedules one message with no application jitter:

BME680 Sensor: Trace requested, please wait up to 60 seconds.

For !hillvue trace 7188, if the known repeater is named Hilltop Repeater, the acknowledgement is instead:

BME680 Sensor: Trace requested to Hilltop Repeater, please wait up to 60 seconds.

The four-character prefix must resolve to exactly one known full public key. The full key is used for authenticated discovery; the name is only a display label. The acknowledgement preserves the full stored display name, including words such as Repeater, independently of compact hop labels. Whitespace is normalized and UTF-8 is kept intact. A known identity without a usable name uses 7188 as its label. An unknown or ambiguous identity retains the existing error and starts neither acknowledgement nor discovery.

Destination, sensor prefix and reply context are frozen when the request is accepted, including during allocation/queue retries. A later rename or cache eviction cannot change that pending request. The acknowledgement stays within one 160-byte public message; if necessary, only the destination label is shortened at a UTF-8 boundary. Bare trace acknowledgement and final result formatting are unchanged.

The entire operation has a fixed 60-second maximum, starting when the command is accepted. It includes acknowledgement, discovery, settling, probes, retries and final reporting. A successful trace finishes early. The final five seconds are reserved for reporting: discovery/probing stops at 55 seconds, and unfinished work becomes Trace: discovery timed out or Trace: no result before timeout. At 60 seconds, remaining queued work is cancelled and the trace slot is released.

Discovery/login stages share the absolute 40-second control cutoff. Probe receive windows share remaining work time: at actual TX start the first probe can use at most half, and the retry the remaining work time, also limited by the ordinary airtime/hop policy below. Queue/CAD/duty delays consume the same fixed budget. An estimated transmission that cannot fit is skipped. Slow/congested links can time out despite being reachable.

The acknowledgement has its own bounded stage. If it cannot be sent, tracing still proceeds after that stage expires. Discovery and probe queue clocks start after the acknowledgement stage. At most one acknowledgement can emit; it does not use another command-rate slot. Invalid requests, duplicates, busy requests, status and cancellation do not create this message.

The overall deadline is fixed when the request is accepted. Replies, retries, status requests and newly observed routes cannot extend it. trace status includes remaining overall seconds and identifies acknowledgement when that is the current stage. trace cancel removes an unsent acknowledgement as well as other queued trace work. On the first running service poll at the overall deadline, the sensor stops further trace work and releases the trace slot. A packet already on air remains under radio ownership until completion/recovery. Channel access and duty limits still apply: neither immediate scheduling nor the advertised maximum guarantees over-air receipt. A blocked application loop also cannot perform cleanup until it runs again.

At most two ordinary discovery requests, three public guest login attempts, and two TRACE probes may emit. The two-probe limit is shared by authenticated and advert routes. Acknowledgement and up to two terminal report parts give at most ten application-originated emitting packets per targeted trace. Discovery/login use durable forward-only request timestamps; random TRACE identifiers remain separate. A short settling window uses the selected loop's estimated airtime. Acknowledgement, discovery/login, settling and queue wait are excluded from RTT.

Transient peer contexts exist only in RAM. Discovery responses do not replace saved management routes or trigger reciprocal PATH traffic. Late and ownerless RESPONSE/PATH replies are ignored after the transaction closes. Normal management requests and non-response PATH handling retain their existing owners. Radio configuration changes cancel queued discovery/probes before further sends. Remaining result parts are stopped on a radio profile change, without issuing a conflicting failure after a result that may already have been transmitted.

MeshCore TRACE does not record timestamps at each repeater, so individual per-node milliseconds cannot be reported from this single probe. The RTT excludes the final repeater-to-companion link, but includes the sensor-to-nearest-repeater link, radio airtime and forwarding delays. Time waiting in the sensor's transmit queue is excluded. It is not a one-way latency or a measurement to the companion. Only one trace runs at a time, including bounded report delivery; paths over ten repeaters are rejected. After acknowledgement, a short airtime-aware settling window before the first probe lets the command flood finish. For bare trace, its earliest start is twice the command airtime, clamped to 300-2000 milliseconds, plus 0-250 milliseconds of jitter. Matching duplicates extend a quiet interval of 150-750 milliseconds, but cannot extend settling past 2.5 seconds. Unrelated messages do not extend it. Settling is excluded from RTT.

Temporary allocation and queue rejections are retried with 250-millisecond, 500-millisecond, then one-second backoff and bounded jitter. Admission is limited to ten seconds per attempt, excluding the initial settling window. A rejected radio start may use the remaining probe attempt, but there are never more than two potentially emitting probe submissions. Local failures do not count as evidence against a route. Once transmission begins, the timeout is the larger of the existing hop allowance and an airtime estimate, rounded up to whole seconds:

Hop allowance:     5000 + 2500 × repeater count
Airtime allowance: 500 + (6 × maximum packet airtime + 250) × (2 × repeater count)

All values are milliseconds. Maximum packet airtime includes the SNR bytes accumulated during the loop. The base minimum is ten seconds for two repeaters, 13 seconds for three, and 30 seconds for ten. Slower radio settings can increase that base allowance; the actual wait is always clamped to the remaining shared work time. Remote repeater congestion cannot be predicted exactly.

After the first trace timeout, if time remains, the sensor makes one silent retry following a random one-to-two-second pause. Bare trace passively watches additional copies of the exact same command for up to three alternate flood paths. Destination trace instead collects additional authenticated PATH responses for the current target and transmitted discovery tags. The original received/discovered route is always tested first. Retry candidates are ranked using recent exact-route outcomes, directed-edge diversity per estimated airtime, freshness and last-hop SNR. Last-hop SNR is not an end-to-end score. Four RAM-only history records expire after fifteen minutes and are scoped to the full transport key, channel and radio configuration. Destination trace also requires the full target public key; bare and destination trace histories remain separate. Temporary radio changes and reversion invalidate old context too. Bare traces with unresolved transport scopes do not reuse history between commands. Destination traces use their selected discovery scope. Alternate copies must match the original command ciphertext and scope. For unresolved scopes, matching also requires the same transport route type and both transport codes; these short codes remain potentially ambiguous and are only conservative hints within that command. A transport-code match to multiple configured keys is treated as unresolved. Region names and IDs are not route-history identities. History only ranks routes observed for the current command: it never invents a route or supplies an old, unobserved path. Bare trace sends no discovery packets. Neither mode treats repeater advert names as network topology. An observed path is a routing hint, not proof that its links work in reverse.

Each attempt has fresh identifiers and retains its own path, hash width and transmission-start time. After acknowledgement, one final result or failure is posted to the requesting channel. A first result received before retry transmission cancels the queued retry. During retry it is retained in RAM as fallback; a successful retry takes precedence. Fallback names and SNRs always describe the first route, even if the retry used another route.

When both probes expire without a result, a three-second final grace period allows either result to arrive, within the 55-second work cutoff. Valid late results before that cutoff can also replace an unsent failure report. Once failure transmission starts, the outcome is committed and late results are ignored, preventing contradictory reports. Failure-report queueing is bounded to ten seconds, including the normal random send delay, and always ends by the original 60-second deadline. The node reports Trace: no result after retry or the applicable timeout stage; it does not claim that no route exists. Radio-busy, transmit-failure and unsent-retry conditions have separate messages. Local recovery never increases the two-probe budget.

Completed results are retained while their reports are prepared and transmitted. Both report parts, including the node-name prefix and cleaned repeater labels, are frozen together. Temporary packet allocation or confirmed queue rejection does not discard a result. Each part has a ten-second admission allowance, and the base success-report allowance is thirty seconds or longer for slow radio airtime, always shortened by the original 60-second transaction deadline. Remaining multipart delivery is best effort within that deadline. The second part remains eligible only three seconds after the first finishes transmitting. An active transmission is left to MeshCore's existing completion/watchdog handling, never freed by the application.

An uncertain report transmission is not repeated: it may already have reached other users. RadioLib start errors are conservatively uncertain because its Boolean result cannot prove that no frame was emitted. A report problem never turns a successful trace into a public trace-failure message. Local transmission completion is not confirmation that the companion received the channel reply. If the owner completion notification is lost, a report observer watchdog releases the trace slot after estimated TX airtime × 1.5 plus one second. It runs after Dispatcher has had its completion/watchdog poll and never frees an in-flight packet. Such delivery is classified as uncertain and is not repeated.

Local diagnostics retain outward and return SNRs, the final received-link SNR, and the furthest matching trace progress overheard for each attempt. Partial progress never completes a trace, extends its timeout or identifies a failed repeater. These snapshots are available to tests/debugger inspection only; the public report averages paired directional readings, and no extra diagnostic traffic is sent.

The original command counts once toward the unchanged four-command-per-minute limit, although a retry sends a second trace packet. Requests received while a trace is running do not use a rate-limit slot; the node sends at most one Trace: already running notice for that trace. Incoming 3-byte path hashes cannot be mirrored by MeshCore TRACE and are reported as unavailable.

After a trace result arrives, its channel reply is scheduled with a one-second minimum plus the usual random 0.5–2-second transmit delay. This spacing does not guarantee a collision-free transmission. The RTT is measured when the trace returns; the reply delay is not included. Repeater labels retain their existing 12-byte UTF-8-safe limit. With the default BME680 Sensor name, all ten repeater lines fit in at most two replies. A longer sensor name may leave too little room; the second reply then ends with ...truncated.

Each selected value appears on its own line in a channel reply; !hillvue and !hillvue all include voltage. A voltage-only request works even when the BME680 is not ready. Before the first voltage sample, or for requested BME680 readings that are not ready, the reply says Sensor data is not ready. During air-quality calibration it reports, for example:

Air Quality: Warming Up (4/10)

A reply that exceeds one message is divided at a line boundary where possible. Both parts carry the sensor's name and are labelled so they can be read in order:

BME680 Sensor: 1/2
Temperature: 22.4 C
Humidity: 48.2%

BME680 Sensor: 2/2
Pressure: 1013.2 hPa
Air Quality: 56/500 (Moderate)

Only two messages are sent for one command. If the reply still does not fit, the second ends with ...truncated; no further parts are sent.

docs.title: Mesh traffic controls
docs.text:
• Commands use the latest cached reading and never trigger an extra sample.
  • The node accepts at most four commands in any rolling 60-second period, shared across all users and commands. This limit is unchanged when a response needs two messages.
  • Responses that do not fit one message are split into at most two, marked 1/2 and 2/2. The second transmission is scheduled at least three seconds after the first one's completed transmission. A busy radio may lengthen the actual gap. Each message is a separate flood, so four accepted commands can produce up to eight reply messages.
  • Hashes for the eight most recent accepted commands are retained in RAM to suppress duplicate packet delivery.
  • The bot does not publish on a schedule and does not respond to its own output.
  • Each response part is sent once as a normal MeshCore flood; the node does not repeat other mesh traffic.

Unknown command options are ignored without a response.

docs.title: Private trace diagnostics
docs.text:
After a failed targeted trace, private/local CLI commands expose the last transaction without transmitting packets or writing storage:

  • get trace.diag: candidate PATH/RESPONSE frames addressed to the sensor with the target's short hash (rx), authenticated response-handler calls (decrypted), accepted login replies (login_reply), recognizable login replies ignored by the state machine, role and route/tag/scope counters.
  • get trace.control 0, get trace.control 1, get trace.control 2: initial discovery, first guest login and final discovery. get trace.control 3 and get trace.control 4 show the two guest-login retries. Each exposes timestamps, request tag and transmission flags. Millisecond timestamps are local uptime. sent=1 means radio TX started; completion without failure is local completion, not an acknowledgement from the repeater.
  • get trace.peer: full target public key, outgoing transport scope key and hash width. An all-zero scope denotes an unscoped flood.

Short-hash candidate matches do not authenticate the remote node. The decrypted counter counts handler calls, not necessarily unique packets. Accepted login replies include unexpected-role replies; consult role and the final failure. A new trace clears these counters. These commands contain no shared secrets, passwords or private keys. They are not public bot commands.

Guest login stops immediately after an accepted reply. An unanswered login or failed transmission may retry, using a fresh durable timestamp each time. Retries are bounded by the original 40-second control and 60-second overall limits, so less than three attempts may fit after long queue delays. Queue expiry, invalid/unexpected granted role, cancellation and clock failure do not start another login. Local allocation/queue admission retries do not count as additional over-air transmissions.

Successful TRACE routes enter volatile route history for 15 minutes. They do not automatically become persistent advert-route entries. An existing matching advert hint can be marked validated in RAM; that outcome alone does not schedule an immediate cache write. Advert-originated paths are persisted through the normal deferred advert-cache save mechanism.

docs.title: Telemetry
docs.text:
Back to README

The node samples the BME680 once every 60 seconds and caches the most recent successful reading. A telemetry request returns cached node and sensor data; it does not trigger an additional BME680 measurement.

Measurement Unit or representation Supply voltage Volts Temperature Degrees Celsius Relative humidity Percent Barometric pressure hPa Calculated altitude Metres Relative air quality 0–500 generic sensor value

The BME680 measurements occupy telemetry channel 2. Node supply voltage uses the standard self-telemetry channel. The same cached battery-voltage reading is available through !hillvue voltage on the Public channel.

docs.title: Altitude
docs.text: Altitude is calculated from barometric pressure using a fixed sea-level reference of 1013.25 hPa, then adjusted by +100 m for the Hillvue installation. Weather-related pressure changes affect the result, so it should be treated as an estimate rather than GPS elevation.

docs.title: Air quality
docs.text:
Air quality combines BME680 gas resistance with humidity compensation. Lower scores represent cleaner air:

Score Rating 0–50 Good 51–100 Moderate 101–150 Poor 151–200 Unhealthy 201–300 Very poor 301–500 Hazardous

The first ten successful samples establish a clean-air baseline. The baseline, sample count and readings remain in RAM and restart after every reboot. This is a relative indicator for observing changes at a fixed installation, not a Bosch BSEC IAQ measurement.

docs.title: Storage
docs.text: Current readings and the air-quality baseline are never written to flash. The node identity, configuration and ACL use the normal MeshCore persistent store. Battery history used by the sensor runtime is also held in RAM.

docs.title: MeshCore 1.18 integration and acceptance record
docs.text:
Release baseline: 81dbae592ffad40b4212bc0b37e82b38da08f4bc, shared by official companion-v1.18.0, repeater-v1.18.0 and room-server-v1.18.0 tags. Validation date: 20 October 2026 (Australia/Sydney).

Status: software integration and automated validation recorded below. Hardware acceptance remains pending. This record does not claim every physical feature has been tested or authorize a production release.

docs.title: Recovery and branch isolation
docs.text:
The local meshcore/main branch was fast-forwarded from d9296435 to the release. The three product branches independently merge that baseline without rebasing or force-pushing. Backup refs retain each original product:

Branch Original commit Backup ref meshcore/main d9296435 backup/pre-1.18-meshcore-main zen/main e35bceea backup/pre-1.18-zen meshcore/sensor 90f9cbcb backup/pre-1.18-sensor meshcore/archiver 981c5872 backup/pre-1.18-archiver

Device rollback requires a saved settings backup and matching previous firmware. Do not assume newer preference files can be read by older firmware. The archive history is intentionally volatile and cannot survive an upgrade/reboot.

docs.title: Integration decisions
docs.text:
• Zen keeps its presentation, message histories, child-mode permissions, notifications, power policies and UI callbacks. The 1.18 listener extension API coexists with this context-rich UI binding. The binding is explicitly retained in the boot composition; replacing it with an unregistered listener would silently disable standalone features.
  • Zen incorporates protocol version 14, local and permitted remote CLI, unsolicited binary responses (including telemetry push), multi-byte raw paths, updated GPS diagnostics and board lifecycle/dynamic preferences. Remote CLI cannot execute while Child Mode is restricted. CLI timezone changes select Zen's fixed-offset mode so clock, quiet time and pet schedules agree.
  • Zen retains repeater Yield x2 and uses the new configurable transmit-delay factors. The new baseline preference fields participate in save suppression; dynamic preference dirty state also forces a baseline save.
  • Sensor retains its application policy hooks, guest telemetry, admin ACL persistence, leaf policy, environmental transformations and public bot. The 1.18 sensor runtime supplies subscriptions, region loading and board hooks. Subscription thresholds are bounds-checked before state mutation; humidity keeps its one-byte, half-percent encoding. Push telemetry reserves its extra timestamp bytes. Custom serial commands use the updated runtime signature.
  • Archiver retains the Public decoder, RAM ring, room snapshot boundaries, hop-dependent history limit, read-only policy and ACK-driven synchronization. Production snapshot selection was extracted into a directly tested policy; normal room-server builds remain free of archive policy.
  • Baseline sources remain exactly upstream in Zen's protected paths. Reviewed overlay counterpart hashes and the sensor boundary pin now reference 1.18. PlatformIO environments, firmware filenames and CI branch tests are retained.

The sensor sanitizer initially could not link because the host's libasan runtime was absent. The matching Fedora runtime was downloaded/extracted under /tmp and the complete instrumented suite was rerun successfully using LIBRARY_PATH and LD_LIBRARY_PATH. No system packages were installed. Stalled dependency clones were replaced with copies of the verified local RadioLib dependency at 6d8934836678d8894e3d556550475b37dce3e2b6.

docs.title: End-to-end release gate (pending)
docs.text:
Use OLED and E-ink Zen devices, the BME680 sensor, the archive, an official 1.18 companion and a 1.17.1 peer. Exercise direct, one-hop and two-plus-hop routes:

  • Poll and subscribe from a companion while sensor bot/trace traffic runs; receive pushed telemetry, unsubscribe and verify expiry.
  • Synchronize archive snapshots from Zen and official companions, including messages arriving during synchronization and all access roles.
  • Verify old saved identities, contacts, channels, ACL, Zen preferences and pet records; export and restore settings before/after flashing.
  • Introduce radio congestion, lost ACKs, disconnect/reconnect, reboot and low power; verify recovery and bounded memory/queues.
  • Run at least 24 hours across a quiet-time boundary and archive wraparound; retain logs, memory readings, traffic observations and device identifiers.

No identifiable supported USB firmware devices were available; the host exposed only generic ttyS entries. Physical display, RF, GPS, sensor, battery, OTA, mixed-firmware interoperability and soak tests are therefore PENDING. Promote/release only after recording those results.

docs.title: Named destination in trace acknowledgement
docs.text:
Status: software implemented and tested; physical acceptance pending. Date: 2026-10-25.

See the validation record.

docs.title: Required behaviour
docs.text:
For a uniquely known target with prefix 7188 and name Hilltop Repeater:

Command: !hillvue trace 7188
Body: Trace requested to Hilltop Repeater, please wait up to 60 seconds.
On air: BME680 Sensor: Trace requested to Hilltop Repeater, please wait up to 60 seconds.

For a known full identity with no usable name:

Trace requested to 7188, please wait up to 60 seconds.

Preserve bare trace exactly:

Trace requested, please wait up to 60 seconds.

Preserve current errors, including the normal sensor-name prefix:

BME680 Sensor: Trace: unknown repeater 7188
BME680 Sensor: Trace: ambiguous repeater 7188

An unknown or ambiguous target starts neither acknowledgement nor discovery. The fallback label applies only to an already resolved full identity; four hex characters alone cannot supply the authenticated discovery public key.

The existing 60-second transaction deadline and 55-second work cutoff remain in force. Displaying a name does not alter discovery, permissions, scope, retry counts, trace routing, averaged SNR, final result formatting or command-rate rules.

docs.title: Current implementation and design decision
docs.text:
RepeaterNameCache stores up to 48 entries containing a full public key and a 32-byte name buffer. resolvePrefix currently returns the unique full key but no name. formatLabel is intended for compact hop labels: it resolves short hashes, removes words such as Repeater, and truncates to its destination buffer. It must not be reused for this acknowledgement, since that would change Hilltop Repeater to Hilltop.

TraceRequestAcknowledgement already copies the entire formatted message, including sensor-name prefix, into a bounded buffer before admission. Keep that ownership model: no pointer into the mutable cache survives acceptance.

docs.title: Implementation sequence
docs.text:
1. Extend the cache lookup with a compatible overload returning the unique full key and a bounded destination display label together. Preserve existing callers and compact path/hop formatting. Resolve both outputs from the same entry in the same lookup; do not look the name up again by a shorter hash.
  2. Clear output key/label on unknown or ambiguous resolution so neither can be accidentally used as a successful lookup. Prefix comparison remains exactly two bytes and uniqueness is based on full identities, not names.
  3. Build the destination display label from the stored full name. Preserve meaningful words, punctuation, case and valid UTF-8, including Repeater. Normalize control characters to spaces, trim leading/trailing whitespace and collapse repeated whitespace for a single-line acknowledgement. Respect the existing stored name limit. Do not change the cache file format or stored names. A name consisting only of whitespace/unsafe or unusable text falls back to the four-character lowercase hex prefix.
  4. In the targeted command branch, complete existing identity/path-width validation before accepting. Pass the local label snapshot into beginAcknowledgement; keep discovery.begin supplied with the full resolved public key. Do not derive protocol identity from a name or fallback label.
  5. Extend acknowledgement formatting with an optional destination argument. Named starts use Trace requested to Y, please wait up to 60 seconds.; absence of that argument preserves the exact bare message. Copy the final text immediately, including destination and sensor prefixes.
  6. Retain zero added application jitter, separate acknowledgement ownership, bounded definitely-unsent retries, and no duplicate after possible emission. Cache rename/eviction, new adverts and sensor rename during queue retry must not change accepted text, identity, reply context or deadline.
  7. Update public bot/developer documentation with named and fallback examples, and record software validation separately from physical acceptance.

docs.title: Message length and encoding policy
docs.text:
The complete text, including sensor-name:, must fit the existing single-part public response limit (160 bytes). Use byte counts and bounded formatting; the terminator requires its own byte. Do not split the acknowledgement.

Preserve the entire fixed message and timeout suffix. If space is constrained, shorten only the destination label at a valid UTF-8 boundary. Prefer the full stored name whenever it fits. If no meaningful destination text fits, try the four-character key-prefix fallback. If even that cannot fit, fail before acceptance through the existing bounded formatting-error path; do not silently omit the destination, produce an empty label or send a truncated timeout.

Normal 31-byte cached names should fit with the normal sensor prefix. Test extreme sensor-prefix lengths explicitly rather than assuming this arithmetic. An entirely unknown nameless advert must retain current cache admission behaviour: the cache currently ignores adverts without a name field. Do not silently expand cache admission merely to exercise the unnamed fallback.

docs.title: Files expected to change
docs.text:
File/area Purpose RepeaterNameCache.h/.cpp Full-identity lookup with full destination label and fallback TraceRequestAcknowledgement.h Optional named destination and bounded one-part formatting SensorBotService.h/.cpp Pass the acceptance snapshot through the targeted start path test_sensor_storage Cache resolution/name/encoding tests test_sensor_trace_ack Exact text, message length, immutability and acknowledgement ownership test_sensor_target_trace Full-key authenticated discovery and unchanged errors test_sensor_network where assertions need extension Named acknowledgement over real simulated links Public bot/development docs and validation record User behaviour and evidence

No changes are expected in core Mesh/Dispatcher, repeater ACL/authentication, cache persistence schema, parser syntax or the 60-second timing policy.

docs.text:

canonical lowercase prefix on fallback Two full keys share 7188 Exact ambiguous error; no acknowledgement, discovery or selected identity Two devices share a name but not key prefix Resolve the requested full key; names do not determine identity Unknown 7188 Exact unknown error; no fallback discovery Known identity, empty/whitespace name Use 7188; discovery still uses all 32 key bytes Advert without a name field Existing cache admission/unknown behaviour is preserved Stored name with controls/repeated whitespace Single-line normalized label; no injected response line UTF-8 and emoji names Preserve valid characters; no split code point at storage/display/message boundaries Invalid/incomplete UTF-8 Bounded usable label or hex fallback; never malformed/truncated output Maximum stored name Full name shown when it fits, rather than the shorter hop-label limit Exact 160-byte message and one-byte overflow Exact-fit succeeds;
