docs.title: Trace first-contact repair and persistent advert fallback
docs.text: Date: 2026-10-25. Implementation in the current working tree on meshcore/sensor above 5add24af. No device has been flashed. Physical acceptance is pending.

docs.title: Implemented
docs.text:
• Separate initial discovery, public guest login, fresh final discovery and passive advert wait phases in the existing TraceDiscovery owner. This is the planned first-contact/login separation implemented with a single current control-packet owner rather than overlapping controllers.
  • One empty public guest attempt by default, configurable locally/privately by get trace.login / set trace.login public|off. No stored/admin password use. Protected guest access, absent replies or unexpected admin grants proceed to advert fallback. No silent denial is presented as proven permission failure.
  • Stock 1.18 login uses the target timestamp and protocol fields. Its route is not committed as discovery. Fresh authenticated request/tag matching is still required. Old login-shaped replies are absorbed separately from discovery.
  • Six/eight/six-second control leases and a 25-second absolute control cutoff; fixed 55-second work cutoff and 60-second transaction deadline; shared total two probes, one login and two ordinary discovery requests. Normal report and averaged-SNR output are preserved.
  • Durable identity-bound timestamp reservations, 256 values per block, two replicated CRC records and read-back validation before use. Reboot skips beyond reserved values; rollback, corrupt storage and write failure cannot reuse uncommitted values. No peer response sets the local wall clock.
  • Verified flooded advert route collection, exact reverse/target/return loop construction for both widths, compact 48-by-two candidates bounded to 10 KiB, scope/radio context and 24-hour known-age expiry. Restored unknown-age hints are probationary and must pass a new TRACE. Alternative routes share the existing probe budget.
  • Separate route-cache sidecar with CRC/identity/version checks, backup recovery, 30-second coalescing and ten-minute save throttling. Only populated entries are serialized; checkpoint replacement keeps at most two route files, with both full caches below 16,000 bytes combined. Existing name persistence and management ACL schemas are unchanged. Temporary-radio observations are not persisted and live candidates are invalidated on configuration changes.
  • Explicit outgoing control scope/default/hash-width selection independent of frozen public reply context. Authenticated full-target/fresh-tag PATH replies may return on a different scope; differences are recorded.
  • Bounded diagnostics: control queue/start/completion evidence and tags, login role, clock health/regression, path rejection and advert/probation provenance. Core pre-decryption failures still require core debug or target-side capture; no visibility is claimed where no service callback exists.

The production repeater login and replay-acceptance logic is shared with the native target through generic RepeaterLogin.h. The stock response encoder is also shared. Production's platform-specific sensor/voltage acquisition remains outside the native target; actual interoperability still needs hardware evidence. The baseline sensor runtime exposes only a protected default-scope value getter; RTC helpers expose hardware detection. No bot policy was added to core Mesh or Dispatcher.

docs.title: Behavioural evidence
docs.text:
New tests exercise:

  • Fresh remote ACL with no sensor entry: initial silence, public guest login, fresh-tag discovery and actual multi-hop TRACE success. The remote guest state is then cleared to model a repeater reboot; the next operation re-establishes it successfully.
  • Protected guest login and unavailable authenticated discovery with a genuine signature-verified advert: login-free fallback still succeeds.
  • Retained filesystem/identity and service recreation without a new advert: persisted hints are loaded as probationary and verified with a new TRACE.
  • Both widths and every route length through ten repeaters, exact outward and return bytes; direct-target hint, invalid signature rejection, alternative route retry, snapshot context and no old result replay.
  • Production-faithful return-scope fallback, including an unknown incoming transport scope processed locally by a target and a default-scope reply. It is accepted while final public context remains frozen.
  • Clock reboot/rollback/forward jump, both-replica commit, missing/corrupt/foreign journal, failed second replica, exhaustion, policy save failure, cache save failure, corrupt-primary backup recovery and full 48-entry repeated checkpoints without a third temporary cache file.
  • Login response padding, missing/wrong identity/data, unexpected role, remote clock regression and fresh ordinary tag ownership; queued-login cancellation and the existing expiry, Dispatcher ownership and packet-pool regressions.

Existing exact-phase fixtures isolate acknowledgement and explicitly select public-login off where that test concerns only ordinary discovery. Their extra radio poll is restricted to initial isolated acknowledgement acceptance, so it cannot alter unrelated multipart queue-boundary timing. Filesystem assertions that previously prohibited every write now specifically prohibit management contact writes: durable timestamp reservations are intentional new trace writes.

Hardware-clock presence supplies the RTC quality flag; this is not an independent attestation of absolute calendar correctness. Previously deployed remote replay floors ahead of locally recoverable time cannot be inferred from silence. Such migration cases may still require trusted time recovery; advert fallback does not require authenticated request timestamps.

docs.title: Validation gates
docs.text:
All final software gates passed:

Gate Result Native, sensor and KISS suites 467/467 passed Sensor AddressSanitizer suite 360/360 passed Five firmware environments, buildprog and UF2 All passed Five DFU archives, CRC and root application manifest/bin/dat Passed Sensor boundaries and whitespace checks Passed Strict MkDocs build Passed; existing FAQ anchor INFO notice remains

The final sensor uses 45,308 bytes of static RAM and 372,388 bytes of flash. Against the preceding named-trace build (37,364 RAM / 360,532 flash), this adds 7,944 RAM and 11,856 flash bytes. Compact route data uses 64-byte hints and 160-byte target entries: a one-target checkpoint is 204 bytes; two full 48-target checkpoints total 15,448 bytes before filesystem overhead. The XIAO framework reserves 28 KiB for InternalFS, so writing populated entries and avoiding a third route checkpoint are material safeguards. Space exhaustion still keeps RAM candidates and the last valid checkpoint rather than discarding management files. A failed timestamp reservation falls back without reusing tags.

The environments were Xiao_nrf52_bme680_sensor, Xiao_nrf52_sensor_baseline, Xiao_nrf52_companion_radio_usb, Xiao_nrf52_repeater, and Xiao_nrf52_room_server. Check summary and artifact hashes record the final outputs. The sensor OTA is .pio/build/Xiao_nrf52_bme680_sensor/MeshCore_BME680_Sensor_Discovery_Repair_OTA_2026-10-25.zip. It is a direct DFU archive, copied from verified firmware.zip, with SHA256 67218cad1e9773a323722d53bd5cad8565c2588fc313fc65f9198b5f97d7e59f.

After installation, get trace.login in the private/local CLI should return > public unless the operator previously selected off. Old named-device records contain no routes: allow verified flooded adverts to warm the new cache before expecting advert-only fallback. The package has not been installed on hardware as part of this work.

ASAN_OPTIONS=detect_leaks=0 pio test -c /tmp/meshcore-scope-asan.ini -e native_sensor_asan

  -e Xiao_nrf52_companion_radio_usb -e Xiao_nrf52_repeater \
  -e Xiao_nrf52_room_server -t buildprog -t create_uf2

git diff --check

The existing isolated ASan configuration uses the extracted host runtime and leak checking disabled, as documented in prior validation. No sanitizer runtime is included in firmware.

Before calling the original field issue resolved, test fresh sensor identity against stock 1.18, known registration, protected guest, advert-only fallback, persistence without an external RTC, remote reboot, scope fallback, a broken first advert route, and cancellation/restart around the 25/55/60-second boundaries. docs.title: Trace guest-login field investigation — 25 October 2026
docs.text:
The later guest-login timing update includes these diagnostics and supersedes this diagnostic-only OTA for testing.

The operator confirmed that 7188 runs MeshCore 1.18, permits blank guest login, and accepts guest login from a companion beside the sensor. The original Discovery Repair OTA still fails: public guest login at 53 seconds remaining, waiting for an advert route at 33 seconds remaining, followed by Trace: guest login not acknowledged. The field problem remains unresolved.

Compared the sensor's anonymous login against BaseChatMesh::sendLogin and the repeater-v1.18.0 tag. The blank credential payload is the same four-byte timestamp with cipher zero padding. Stock 1.18 accepts an unknown full identity with the configured blank guest password. The stock reply uses the server timestamp, zero response code and keepalive byte, admin flag, ACL permissions, nonce and firmware level, matching the sensor parser. This does not prove over-air receipt.

Transport differences remain: the companion can use a saved direct path and selected/default send scope; the sensor floods and can inherit the public command scope when it has no explicit default scope. The sensor also applies fixed stage leases encompassing queue, transmission and response. Neither observation proves the cause on this particular deployment. No credential, scope, retry or timing changes were made in this diagnostic follow-up.

Added private/local get trace.diag, get trace.peer and get trace.control 0|1|2. The readouts retain the last transaction until a new trace, perform no I/O writes or sends, and fit the existing 160-byte CLI reply contract. Candidate packet counts use short hashes and are not authentication. Authenticated handler counts can include multiple calls for a frame. Accepted login replies include unexpected-role responses; inspect role and final error. A successful local TX is not proof the repeater received it. No physical radio capture, flashing, or hardware acceptance was performed here.

Validation: all 362 native_sensor tests passed, including two new diagnostics regressions. Xiao_nrf52_bme680_sensor firmware/DFU/UF2 build, strict MkDocs, sensor-boundary check and git diff --check passed. ZIP CRC, manifest application BIN/DAT presence validated. Prior named repair archive retained unchanged.

Diagnostic OTA: .pio/build/Xiao_nrf52_bme680_sensor/MeshCore_BME680_Sensor_Trace_Login_Diagnostics_OTA_2026-10-25.zip. SHA256: 5514bc846258643f44816786792871bf91a461cbce87af21bce558090b4fa4cb.

After reproducing once, collect get trace.diag, get trace.control 1, get trace.peer before starting another trace. If the login exchange is locally complete but no candidate reply is seen, a capture of the sensor and companion exchanges or repeater-side reception is still required to separate forward-path failure, repeater processing and return-path failure.

docs.title: Two guest-login retries — 25 October 2026
docs.text:
Guest login now allows an initial attempt and two retries: at most three login transmissions per targeted trace. An unanswered reply window or failed TX can advance to the next attempt after bounded backoff (250 then 500 ms). Every submitted login uses a fresh timestamp from the existing durable clock. Local allocation/admission retries remain within the current queue lease.

An accepted reply stops further logins and enables the second ordinary path-discovery request. Invalid/unexpected roles, clock failure, queue expiry, cancellation, exhausted attempts and the control cutoff do not generate more logins. Protected guest access is tested through all three attempts and still permits successful advert fallback. Cancellation and stale callbacks retain existing ownership protections.

Each attempt retains a separate eight-second queue allowance, airtime-based TX watchdog and up to eight seconds for the acknowledgement after successful local TX completion. The control cutoff moves from 25 to 40 seconds from acceptance to accommodate three reply windows plus ordinary discovery. All phases are clipped to that cutoff; arbitrary queue delays can prevent all attempts fitting. The original 55-second work and 60-second overall deadlines remain. This leaves 15 seconds after the latest control cutoff for probe work and five for final reporting; long routes are not guaranteed to complete within the hard cap.

At most ten application-originated packets can emit: two discovery requests, three logins, two TRACE probes, one acknowledgement and two report parts. Diagnostics preserve slots 0/1/2 (initial discovery, first login, final discovery) and add slots 3/4 for the two login retries. Status includes login attempt N/3.

Path persistence is unchanged: successful trace results update RAM-only route history (15-minute TTL). A newly discovered path is not inserted into the persistent advert-route cache. An already matching advert hint is marked as validated in RAM; that outcome alone does not schedule a flash checkpoint. Advert-derived hints persist via the existing deferred advert-cache saves.

Four new regressions cover exactly three attempts with independent receive windows, stopping on second-attempt success, absolute cutoff/cancellation, and three real Dispatcher transmissions using distinct durable timestamps. Existing single-login timeout tests now expect the bounded retry state. Protected-target integration expects three login requests. Busy/status tests explicitly advance polls or the updated control deadline rather than relying on the old cutoff.

Validation logs:

  • /tmp/trace-login-retries-all-tests.log: native, native_sensor, native_kiss_modem.
  • /tmp/trace-login-retries-asan.log: existing isolated native_sensor_asan config, ASAN_OPTIONS=detect_leaks=0.
  • /tmp/trace-login-retries-build.log: Xiao_nrf52_bme680_sensor buildprog + create_uf2.
  • Strict MkDocs, sensor-boundary integration check and git diff --check.

OTA: .pio/build/Xiao_nrf52_bme680_sensor/MeshCore_BME680_Sensor_Trace_Login_Retries_OTA_2026-10-25.zip. SHA256: fce20672fec24d85e510de37f018d624bfedf7ebcc06051296c71319037157e8. Archive CRC/root manifest/application BIN/DAT validated. Named archive equals the current firmware.zip; earlier named OTA packages remain untouched. No hardware was flashed. Successful discovery/login with repeater 7188 remains unconfirmed.

docs.title: Guest-login reply timing — 25 October 2026
docs.text:
Superseded by the two-retry update, which retains the post-completion reply window and increases the control cutoff to 40 seconds.

The guest-login stage previously had one eight-second lease covering queueing, transmission and the reply. A valid acknowledgement could therefore arrive after that lease despite responding promptly to the actual transmission. This is a confirmed timing limitation, not proof of the cause of 7188's field failure.

Guest login now uses three distinct phases:

  1. Queue admission/dispatch: at most eight seconds.
  2. Transmission: cached airtime watchdog (airtime * 1.5 + 1000 ms) starting at actual radio TX start.
  3. Receive: up to eight seconds starting at successful local TX completion.

Each phase is clipped to the original 25-second control cutoff from command acceptance. A completion close to that cutoff has less than eight seconds for its reply. The 55-second work cutoff and 60-second overall promise remain. Ordinary discovery leases, login count, credentials and scope selection are unchanged. The private diagnostic readouts remain included.

TX completion must match the owned in-flight packet. Missing or failed TX, queue expiry, cancellation and expired TX/control leases never arm receive. Duplicate or late completion cannot renew a receive window. trace status distinguishes guest login queued, transmitting and awaiting reply with the current phase's remaining time. A TX watchdog expiry is a transmission failure, not a claim that the repeater ignored the credential.

Six new regressions cover queue/airtime separation, the exclusive receive boundary, missing/late/wrong/duplicate completion, cancellation and queue expiry, 25-second clipping across millisecond wrap, and a real Dispatcher with a busy channel. In that packet-level test login starts at 13.2 seconds, completes at 13.3 seconds and receives its authenticated reply at 19 seconds; the old combined stage lease would have ended at 14.2 seconds. The new implementation accepts the reply and queues fresh discovery without another login.

Validation: 475/475 regression tests and 368/368 sanitizer tests passed.

Commands and logs:

  • pio test -e native -e native_sensor -e native_kiss_modem: /tmp/trace-login-timing-all-tests.log.
  • ASAN_OPTIONS=detect_leaks=0 pio test -c /tmp/meshcore-scope-asan.ini -e native_sensor_asan: /tmp/trace-login-timing-asan.log. Existing isolated local ASan runtime/config.
  • pio run -e Xiao_nrf52_bme680_sensor -t buildprog -t create_uf2: /tmp/trace-login-timing-build.log; passed.
  • Strict MkDocs, sensor-boundary check and git diff --check: passed.
  • OTA ZIP CRC, root manifest and application BIN/DAT presence validated; built HEX/UF2 nonempty. The new archive is byte-for-byte equal to firmware.zip. Earlier named archives were preserved.

OTA: .pio/build/Xiao_nrf52_bme680_sensor/MeshCore_BME680_Sensor_Trace_Login_Timing_OTA_2026-10-25.zip. SHA256: a34a99560b5a2f53a03d6d184b0f161136bc8049904b67d55000633451f8747a.

No hardware was flashed and 7188 interoperability is not yet confirmed. If this still fails, use the private/local diagnostics after one failed trace, before starting another: get trace.diag, get trace.control 1, get trace.peer.

docs.title: Trace recovery review and fixes
docs.text: Date: 25 October 2026 (Australia/Sydney). Reviewed baseline: 69891ef8 (More trace functionality). No device was flashed.

docs.title: Reported symptom and conclusion
docs.text:
The user ran !hillvue trace 4df5 again after thirty seconds and received a busy reply. That observation matches the configured discovery wait; by itself it does not demonstrate a deadlock. The target must already recognise and permit the sensor identity, independently of whether the requesting phone can contact it. No device logs, active radio settings or over-air capture were supplied, so a physical failure of repeater 4df5 has not been established.

The discovery receive allowance uses the estimated airtime of a maximum 255-byte packet and the ten-repeater trace policy. Under shipped SF8/BW62.5/CR5, CRC/explicit-header and 32-symbol-preamble assumptions, the repository's RadioLib formula gives about 1,512 ms maximum-frame airtime. The policy then gives 187,000 ms per discovery attempt: about six minutes fourteen seconds for two unanswered attempts, plus admission and reporting delays. Saved device radio preferences can change that. The former constant-100-ms radio fixtures exercised only the 30-second minimum and did not make the real-world wait obvious.

The conservative receive allowance has not been shortened without physical latency evidence. The firmware now exposes the actual current-phase allowance and lets the operator stop waiting without rebooting.

docs.title: Findings and changes
docs.text:
Priority Finding Resolution High, demonstrated by fault injection TraceReportDelivery::expired() unconditionally excluded active transmissions. Losing the owner completion notification could keep trace_report.active() and the shared busy flag set forever, even after Dispatcher released the packet. Cache a TX observer budget before transmission: estimated frame airtime × 1.5 plus 1,000 ms grace. Evaluate the fallback only after Dispatcher gets its normal completion/watchdog poll. Close application state as uncertain, with no re-send or contradictory failure. Never release an in-flight packet from the application. Medium Terminal discovery FAILED was excluded from the busy flag. A new bare command arriving exactly at second queue expiry could be admitted, then cancelled by the previous discovery failure handler using the new command's context. Keep discovery failure owned until its error report is scheduled. Advance discovery deadlines before processing the next received command. Medium Unsigned elapsed subtraction could expire a newly created report if its begin timestamp was newer than a cached loop timestamp. This can drop the error/result that explains an operation's outcome. Check signed wrap-safe report age, refresh loop time after work, and use a fresh timestamp for report expiry. Future inter-part due times remain valid. Medium Bare queued probes were invalidated after the runtime radio loop, allowing a send on changed radio settings. Pending reports could also carry a cached TX allowance into another profile. Validate all active trace forms before radio dispatch. Drop remaining result parts on profile change without issuing a conflicting second terminal message. Advance the captured profile when scheduling a configuration-change failure so it cannot recreate itself forever. Hardening A null TX callback could advance an unsubmitted discovery because both pointers were null. Ignore null start/failure notifications; keep the start observer free of radio/SPI estimates by using the previously cached budget. Operator visibility A single generic busy notice did not distinguish discovery from probing/report delivery, and there was no channel cancellation command. Add phase/attempt/remaining-time information, explicit status and cancellation controls.

The first three reproductions were added before their fixes and failed on the reviewed code. The missing-notification reproduction suppresses the service's completion callback while allowing real Dispatcher/pool completion, then tries a second trace. This is a software fault-injection result, not evidence that the same notification was lost on the user's hardware.

docs.title: Operator commands
docs.text:
!hillvue trace status
!hillvue trace cancel
!hillvue trace 4df5

Status shows idle, discovery, settling, probe or report delivery. Discovery and probe status include the attempt and current queue/receive time remaining. The first busy discovery notice now includes those details as well. Status is a snapshot taken when the command is processed; reply queue time can make it older.

Cancellation removes owned queued discovery/probe/report work, stops retries and future report parts, and releases the shared trace slot. Its acknowledgement uses the cancelling command's channel and scope. Already-emitted packets cannot be recalled, and Dispatcher retains exclusive ownership of any in-flight packet. Late replies cannot restart the cancelled transaction or modify management ACL routes. Starting another trace still obeys the normal four-command-per-minute limit. Status and idle cancel requests use that limit; active cancellation is permitted even if its normal command slots are exhausted, with at most one cancel acknowledgement per rate-limited operation.

docs.title: Scope of review and tests
docs.text:
Reviewed command grammar/rate limiting, target resolution, authenticated peer ownership, discovery queue/wait/retired states, passive/discovered candidates, full-target/scope history, probe retries/fallback/grace, signed directional SNR pairing, report queue/TX/multipart lifecycle, callback routing, pool ownership, radio generation changes, and production loop ordering.

New regressions cover:

  • The reported thirty-second busy observation, plus a realistic 1,512 ms max-frame airtime fixture showing discovery 1/2 with 158 seconds remaining when queried at thirty seconds.
  • New commands arriving at discovery expiry and a missing report completion notification, followed by successful admission of another trace.
  • Restart and full pool recovery after success, discovery timeout, queue exhaustion, rejected start, probe timeout, and unsent report expiry.
  • Status/idle controls, cancellation of queued discovery, waiting discovery, a bare probe and queued report, and a new transaction despite old late replies.
  • Cancel acknowledgement channel/scope and cancellation under exhausted normal rate slots, without allowing unlimited idle cancellation replies.
  • Stale timestamps, millis wrap, explicit TX callback budgets and no radio estimate inside the TX-start observer.
  • Delayed-but-successful completion polling preserving the second report part; queued/in-flight results and bare probes across radio profile changes.

docs.title: Physical acceptance and remaining uncertainty
docs.text:
Not run. No device was flashed. Install the corrected firmware and confirm 4df5's ACL/telemetry permission for the sensor's full identity and the actual radio parameters. Verify status countdown, cancel-and-restart after thirty seconds, eventual timeout with an intentionally non-responding target, successful routing, scope retention, TX completion/multipart delivery and late replies on a controlled mesh. Compare RTT and directional average SNR with captures.

This review establishes the software recovery faults and fixes; it does not establish that the user's thirty-second busy reply was caused by an indefinite lock, a remote permission failure or a physical radio problem. Hardware/OTA installation remains a separate acceptance gate.

docs.title: Trace request acknowledgement validation
docs.text:
Historical pre-cap record: its calculated maximum and artifact hashes are superseded by the 60-second cap validation.

Date: 2026-10-25. Implementation is in the current working tree on top of 69891ef8, including the existing trace recovery changes. No commit, device flash, or over-air acceptance is implied by this record.

docs.title: Implemented behaviour
docs.text:
Accepted bare and targeted trace requests schedule one acknowledgement without application jitter:

BME680 Sensor: Trace requested, please wait up to X seconds.

The text, name prefix, reply channel, scope and path-hash width are captured. The acknowledgement owns separate state from the final result. Its admission lease is ten seconds; after TX start, it uses the actual packet's cached TX watchdog, checked against the planned maximum-frame allowance. Only definitely unsent failures can retry. Missing callbacks, allocation failure and queue rejection cannot hold the acknowledgement stage indefinitely. Tracing proceeds when that stage finishes, even if acknowledgement failed.

The fixed overall deadline is anchored at acceptance. Its checked 64-bit budget includes acknowledgement, optional two-attempt discovery, settling, two probe attempts/admissions, retry pause, final grace and terminal delivery. Bare traces reserve their original route for attempt one and the maximum supported route for a fresh alternate; destination traces reserve maximum routes before discovery. Displayed seconds round up. Unrepresentable budgets are rejected. New probe/discovery phases reserve terminal-report time; expiry does not open a new reporting window. Status shows remaining overall seconds.

Queue cleanup runs before Dispatcher admission. Transmission observation gets normal completion/watchdog polling first. Cancellation, profile changes and expiry cancel only owned queued packets. In-flight allocation stays under Dispatcher ownership. The software releases trace ownership on the first running service poll at expiry; receipt under RF loss or a stopped application loop cannot be guaranteed.

The timing calculation uses the conservative composition in the approved plan. For representative shipped SF8/BW62.5/CR5 estimates, a destination trace advertises 617 seconds; a bare three-repeater example advertises 164 seconds. Stored settings determine the actual value. These maxima intentionally include failure paths and are longer than normal successful runs.

docs.title: Coverage
docs.text:
test_sensor_trace_ack contains 54 cases covering:

  • Independent numeric fast/slow budget examples; checked overflow/invalid input; rounding boundaries; all ten supported route lengths and both hash widths.
  • Exact deadline and rollover behaviour, skipped polls, and refusing a new full phase when too little time remains.
  • Real encryption/Dispatcher acknowledgement before probe and discovery; unchanged RTT/SNR result output; slow acknowledgement not consuming probe admission time.
  • Allocation pressure, busy-channel delay, queue rejection, definitely unsent failures, uncertain emission, and lost completion callbacks.
  • Cancellation queued/on air, radio-profile invalidation, duplicates/busy starts, invalid routes/unknown target, status and restart after expiry.
  • Frozen prefix despite queue retry; oversized prefix rejection; frozen channel, scope and width across both channels, both widths and scoped/unscoped requests.

Older exact-phase integration tests explicitly isolate acknowledgement via a transport seam to preserve their probe/report boundary characterization. The new acknowledgement suite and network suites disable that seam and use real Dispatcher ownership. Existing parser/rate-limit, target discovery, averaged SNR, late-result fallback, history, two-part reporting and cancellation regressions also run.

The network simulation delivers acknowledgements separately from terminal reports, including scoped relays and both channels/widths. Its collision case shows that an acknowledgement flood can make an otherwise valid two-byte route need the second allowed attempt. Success remains required, with at most two probe transmissions. This is an RF contention consideration for hardware acceptance, not proof of physical radio performance.

docs.title: Hardware acceptance still pending
docs.text: No connected sensor/repeater hardware was used and no firmware was installed. Verify the plan's physical matrix before treating RF behaviour as accepted: reachable/silent 4df5, bare trace, both channels and scopes, direct/multi-hop, fast/slow profiles, contention, cancellation and lost final replies. Record acceptance/TX/result/cleanup timestamps and compare them to the frozen displayed maximum. Re-run the original second-request-after-30-seconds scenario: busy before the advertised deadline can be correct; busy persisting after deadline cleanup on a running loop is a failure. Confirm the next trace starts without a reboot. Actual link SNR and receipt require hardware evidence.

docs.title: Sensor trace scope implementation validation
docs.text: Date: 24 October 2026 (Australia/Sydney). Revision: working tree based on 99dc1448 on meshcore/sensor.

docs.title: Implemented behaviour
docs.text:
• Replies capture the selected transport key, channel and path-hash width when accepted. Ordinary multipart replies, trace success/failure reports, delayed fallback, busy notices and allocation/queue retries retain their own context.
  • Recognised scope is mirrored; explicitly unscoped floods remain unscoped; unresolved/direct requests use the usable default, otherwise unscoped. Pending replies retain their captured selection across default changes or region removal. Transport codes are computed from each new reply payload.
  • Candidate matching and the four-entry, fifteen-minute RAM history are scoped by the complete resolved transport key. Unresolved scopes do not reuse history; within a transaction their copies must match both transport codes and route class as well as command ciphertext. Short-code ambiguity remains possible, so these are conservative hints rather than proven node identities.
  • Region resolution uses the packet being observed and performs no persistent writes. Multiple configured keys matching one short code are treated as unresolved. Names/region IDs are not history identities.
  • The production and native runtimes instantiate the same SensorScopeBinding. Generic capture/selection/send helpers are shared with the upstream sensor; bot-specific context stays in the BME680 application. The trace packet format, two-attempt limit, timeout policy and conservative failure wording are retained.

docs.title: Automated validation
docs.text:
Check Result native, native_sensor, native_kiss_modem 247/247 passed native_sensor_asan 141/141 passed; no address-sanitizer findings Final report-direction negative controls and pool recovery assertions 30/30 passed in both regular and ASan sensor environments Sensor boundary check Passed git diff --check Passed mkdocs build --strict Passed

The new suites are selected by the existing test_sensor_* CI filter and its sanitizer inheritance. These are local runs of the CI checks; no remote CI run or publication was initiated. Native clean compilation retains existing Crypto library endianness macro/no-hardware-RNG warnings. Firmware retains the project's existing -w build flag. MkDocs reports an existing FAQ anchor issue at INFO level, without failing strict validation.

The recorded check summaries contain the test suite and firmware results.

The regular checks use:

pio test -e native -e native_sensor -e native_kiss_modem
bash bin/check-sensor-boundaries.sh

The sensor sanitizer checks use the existing native_sensor_asan source and flags with ASAN_OPTIONS=detect_leaks=0, as documented by the project. The host compiler's ASan linker script pointed at a missing system library, so the first attempt could not link. Validation downloaded and extracted the matching Fedora libasan-16.2.1-2.fc44.x86_64 RPM under /tmp, without installing a system package. A temporary copy of the project configuration adds only the local library search path/rpath and an isolated build directory:

ASAN_OPTIONS=detect_leaks=0 pio test \
  -c /tmp/meshcore-scope-asan.ini -e native_sensor_asan

The temporary config uses -L/tmp/meshcore-scope-asan-runtime/usr/lib64, -Wl,-rpath,/tmp/meshcore-scope-asan-runtime/usr/lib64, and build_dir = /tmp/meshcore-scope-asan-build. No sanitizer was disabled beyond existing leak detection policy. The temporary sanitizer build directory is isolated so local configuration changes do not invalidate firmware outputs.

New regression coverage includes five focused Dispatcher lifecycle tests, eighteen scope integration/binding tests, four scope/history candidate tests and four scoped network-medium cases. Existing coverage continues to exercise pool reuse, cancellation, expiry, uncertain sends, temporary radio changes, late-result fallback, ambiguity display and physical-path geometry.

docs.title: Physical acceptance
docs.text:
Not run. No device was flashed. Automated packet-medium tests cannot verify physical delivery, actual RF contention, RTT timing or directional SNR order.

The implementation plan remains the physical checklist: scoped delivery through relays rejecting unscoped floods; both channels and hash widths; delayed multipart and default scope changes; slower radio and contention timing; retry/fallback without contradictory reports; outward-hop SNR order; telemetry/admin persistence and UF2/OTA update smoke tests. Record physical results independently before marking hardware acceptance complete.

docs.title: Sensor versus Zen trace discovery: read-only review
docs.text:
Historical pre-implementation findings. See the subsequent repair implementation and validation.

Date: 2026-10-25. Sensor: meshcore/sensor at 5add24af. Zen comparison: local zen/main at 6ba09b28. No firmware, test source, configuration, identity, ACL or radio settings changed. Only this review document was added. No network request/login was performed.

docs.title: Conclusion and confidence
docs.text:
The sensor sends the same authenticated telemetry-based path discovery as Zen, but it assumes the destination already knows the sensor's full identity. The sensor does not establish that prerequisite. Stock MeshCore 1.18 cannot decrypt this request from an unknown client because the packet carries only a short sender hash. Learning a repeater's advert/name/public key on the sensor does not register the sensor on that repeater.

User evidence for 7188: it runs MeshCore 1.18, Zen has previously logged into it, and the sensor has not knowingly been registered or logged in. This strongly supports missing remote client registration as the cause for 7188. It is a confirmed protocol/design gap under an unregistered-sensor setup, not a remotely observed ACL inspection or packet-level proof of this specific failure.

The user also reports Zen success with repeaters they have never had access to. That observation remains valid and unresolved: administrator access is not required for this telemetry request, and guest/client identity knowledge differs from admin access. However, the current Zen trace entry point itself performs no automatic login either. Static code cannot establish those other repeaters' client tables, earlier traffic, exact firmware, or the installed Zen build. Do not claim that a prior guest login definitely occurred. Capture the successful Zen transaction and compare it to sensor traffic to settle this discrepancy.

Additional confirmed differences are outgoing scope/width selection and strict sensor reply-scope filtering. A clock-reset replay failure is another concrete conditional risk. No evidence establishes either as the deployed cause yet.

docs.title: Protocol comparison
docs.text:
Stage Sensor Zen Destination Unique four-hex prefix resolves a full cached 32-byte key Selected repeater's full 32-byte key/contact Discovery type PAYLOAD_TYPE_REQ PAYLOAD_TYPE_REQ Plaintext RTC tag, 03 FE 00 00 00, four random bytes Same fields and sizes Request size 13 plaintext bytes before encryption/padding Same Shared secret self_id.calcSharedSecret(secret, target_key) ContactInfo::getSharedSecret, which calls the same operation Source on wire Sender identity hash, not its full public key Same Outgoing login inside trace None None Send scope Captured bot request/reply scope, default fallback when unresolved Current send_unscoped / send_scope / configured default scope Flood hash width Incoming bot command's width Zen's configured path_hash_mode + 1 Expected route reply Authenticated PATH with embedded RESPONSE and matching tag Same Reply eligibility Full target, sent tag, current owner/profile/time and exact captured scope Full target, sent tag and active session; no equivalent reply-scope comparison in pathResponse Timing Existing hop/airtime policy clamped into 55-second work / 60-second total Flood timeout from actual request airtime plus grace Initial public acknowledgement Yes, separate radio transmission No corresponding public-channel ACK

The payload fields are equivalent in the compared source. No random trace-ID / RTC-tag mixup was found. The added public acknowledgement can affect airtime and contention, but normal discovery response matching begins only after actual request TX start, and the current budget leaves far more than the reported one-second successful Zen discovery under ordinary settings.

docs.title: Finding 1: unknown requesters cannot use this authenticated discovery
docs.text:
Evidence:

  • examples/bme680_sensor/SensorScopeBinding.h:50-59 creates a normal encrypted request; there is no anonymous login or full sender key in its application data.
  • src/Mesh.cpp:492-509 serializes destination hash, source hash and ciphertext.
  • src/Mesh.cpp:151-160 asks searchPeersByHash for candidate shared secrets before decrypting any ordinary request.
  • examples/simple_repeater/MyMesh.cpp:623-637 searches the repeater ACL only. With no matching client, there is no decryption candidate and no request reply.
  • examples/simple_repeater/MyMesh.cpp:663-687 handles a known client's request, checks replay freshness and creates the PATH response for a flooded request.
  • examples/simple_repeater/MyMesh.cpp:240-260 permits guest base telemetry; this is not an administrator-only operation.
  • examples/simple_repeater/MyMesh.cpp:650-659 observes repeater neighbours but does not turn incoming sensor adverts into registered requester clients.

The normal first-contact mechanism is an encrypted PAYLOAD_TYPE_ANON_REQ login. Its packet includes the full sender public key, allowing the recipient to derive a shared secret before the requester is in its ACL. A valid configured guest login can establish a transient client entry; it does not require admin privileges. Bad/disabled guest credentials can be silently ignored, so an absent login reply alone must not be labelled proof of permission denial.

Zen has a general login path (BaseChatMesh::sendLogin) and the user confirms using it on 7188. Its trace path is UITask::startRepeaterTrace -> MyMesh::startRepeaterTrace -> RepeaterTraceSession::start -> authenticated telemetry flood. That sequence does not itself call login. Accordingly, simply copying more of Zen's request builder will not fill the sensor's first-contact gap.

docs.title: Finding 2: scope is neither selected nor accepted identically
docs.text:
Outgoing policy differs:

  • Sensor SensorScopeBinding.h:64-75 captures context from the bot packet; src/helpers/RegionScope.h preserves a resolved request scope, keeps an unscoped flood unscoped, or uses the configured default for unresolved scope.
  • Zen MyMesh.cpp:746-770 on the compared branch uses its local flood-scope override/default and local path-hash-width preference.

The public #hillvue channel and a transport region are separate concepts. Receiving the command on the same channel does not prove the subsequent sensor and Zen discovery frames use the same transport key or scope mode.

The sensor then silently returns from SensorBotService.cpp:660-662 when a matching authenticated PATH response uses a different scope/mode. Zen's RepeaterTraceSession::pathResponse has no equivalent scope comparison.

A concrete conditional divergence: a target directly hears a request whose transport scope it does not resolve, processes it locally, and emits a reply using its own default scope or no scope. The stock repeater's onRecvPacket sets recv_pkt_region but still calls core Mesh processing; the region gate is on forwarding. sendFloodReply selects a default when request scope is unresolved. Sensor may decrypt and silently reject that response; Zen may accept an equivalently authenticated response if it reaches the device.

For a correctly resolved matching scope, stock 1.18 normally mirrors it; this is not proof of a defect on every scoped trace. Record actual outgoing and return modes/keys before changing policy. Do not indiscriminately accept all foreign-scope replies to conceal the discrepancy. Explicitly decide whether trace discovery should retain strict captured-scope semantics or match Zen's less restrictive response policy.

docs.title: Finding 3: RTC tags are correct in-process, not guaranteed across reboot
docs.text:
Both implementations use getCurrentTimeUnique for discovery. The sensor's uniqueTime adapter calls the real RTC helper, so the old random-ID integration mistake is not present here.

However, src/MeshCore.h:119-124 only guarantees increasing values within the current clock object's lifetime. variants/xiao_nrf52/target.cpp:16-22 uses an auto-discovered RTC with VolatileRTCClock fallback. Without a supported external RTC or later clock synchronization, ArduinoHelpers.h:11 starts that fallback at 2024-05-15 on each reset. A registered sender that previously sent higher timestamps can then be rejected by timestamp > client->last_timestamp on a still-running repeater. Wrong absolute time alone is insufficient to prove a replay failure: it must be at or below that same client's recorded timestamp.

Tests use a valid advancing synthetic RTC and do not cover this complete production reboot/remote-retained-client scenario. Compare both actual sensor time and transmitted tag to the remote per-client value. Do not solve replay rejection with random tags or unconditional trust in a peer's reported clock.

docs.title: Finding 4: prior success tests assumed registration
docs.text:
TargetedSensorNetwork::SetUp at test/test_sensor_network.cpp:571-573 explicitly adds sensor_mesh->self_id as a guest on the remote before every success case. It supplies the correct shared secret too. The mock target implements the request/replay/PATH response subset, not the complete production repeater login and telemetry handler.

UnknownRemoteClientTimesOutWithoutAutomaticLogin deliberately removes that remote ACL entry, then expects discovery timeout and no trace. This confirms the behaviour but does not satisfy a user expectation that a newly deployed sensor can discover any known repeater. Earlier passing test totals therefore did not validate first-contact operation. This is a gap in the implementation's intended behaviour and its acceptance coverage.

Wrong-scope tests likewise deliberately assert sensor rejection, while normal network successes use one shared scope throughout. They do not establish that real 1.18 reply-scope fallback matches the sensor's assumption.

docs.title: Paths checked without a matching defect found
docs.text:
• Full destination keys are resolved and passed to encryption, not four hex characters treated as a complete key. Ambiguous prefixes are rejected.
  • Base telemetry mask is ~1, matching Zen's ~TELEM_PERM_BASE.
  • Reserved bytes and random nonce positions match; packet padding is handled by the shared core encryption/decryption routines.
  • Discovery ownership is installed after queueing and before the asynchronous Dispatcher can start TX. Production callbacks forward TX start/completion/ failure into the service. No missing binding was found.
  • Transient target peers supplement the sensor's management ACL lookup and are used to decrypt returning PATH replies. An existing matching ACL peer can still dispatch to discovery without saving a management route.
  • Both implementations construct the loop from the target's embedded outbound path, append the target hash, and reverse intermediate hops for the return leg.
  • Late response absorption and retired target/tag ownership are deliberate and do not substitute an old cached route for a fresh discovery.
  • Differences in discovery timeout formulas cannot explain a normal one-second reply never being accepted under the ordinary current sensor time windows.
  • Core branch differences reviewed include PATH bounds checks and safer TRACE path validation; neither shows a normal valid 1.18 PATH reply being rejected solely because those safety checks exist.

docs.title: Read-only validation performed
docs.text:
Ran the existing suites without editing test source:

/home/matt/.platformio/penv/bin/pio test -e native_sensor \
  --filter test_sensor_target_trace --filter test_sensor_network

109/109 tests passed. This includes known-client success, unknown-client expected failure, replay protection, full-key matching, wrong-scope rejection and real Dispatcher/network timing. No new reproduction tests were implemented, and no over-air evidence or target ACL contents were collected during this review. Build products/logs may be refreshed by that test command; firmware source is unchanged.

docs.title: Recommended repair and verification sequence
docs.text:
1. Confirm the comparison uses the same full target key, actual deployed build versions and PHY settings. Read the relevant target client ACL locally or capture target-side request handling. Never infer ACL state solely from the sensor knowing the target's name or from prior admin access on another device.
  2. Capture one working Zen attempt and one failing sensor attempt. Record packet types in order (including any anonymous login before discovery), sender and target identities, actual TX times, scope mode/fingerprint, hash width, request timestamp and whether a PATH response was emitted. Do not log shared secrets or passwords.
  3. Track the sensor receive checkpoints: matching source/destination, MAC/decrypt success, tag ownership, active phase/profile, scope acceptance, route decode and first probe admission. Existing timeout text does not distinguish these silent exits; add bounded RAM/debug evidence in a separately authorized fix.
  4. Implement a bounded first-contact strategy for targets that do not know the sensor, using only the target's configured guest-access policy. Prefer an explicitly owned guest login followed by a fresh ordinary discovery request. Do not elevate to admin or silently guess passwords. Both stages must share the existing 60-second total and preserve cancellation and packet ownership.
  5. Handle login as its own protocol: stock login replies begin with the target's timestamp and RESP_SERVER_LOGIN_OK, not an echo of the discovery request tag (MyMesh.cpp:135-144). Feeding that response through current tag matching would still fail. Correlate it using the correct selected identity/state and protocol semantics, then send a new, fresh-tag discovery. Avoid introducing stale login replies or new management-route side effects.
  6. Resolve any measured scope difference deliberately, with tests against real stock request/reply selection. Keep public reply context independent if outbound discovery scope becomes a separate policy; preserve captured final report channel/scope semantics.
  7. Add an explicit registered-client reboot/replay test and clock validity diagnostics before choosing a persistent monotonic-time strategy. Do not assume a successful login repairs a stale subsequent request timestamp.

Essential new tests for an eventual fix:

  • Fresh sensor, empty remote ACL, allowed guest login, then authenticated PATH discovery and successful trace, with no test pre-registration.
  • Guest access unavailable/restricted: bounded stage-specific outcome without claiming RF failure or explicit permission denial from silence alone.
  • Remote restart loses transient guest state: next sensor operation re-establishes it within the same deadline and emits bounded traffic.
  • Sensor reboot rolls back fallback RTC while the target retains higher replay state; detect/report this accurately and exercise the chosen clock policy.
  • Valid reply on same scope, target default fallback scope, unscoped fallback, and deliberately foreign scope; compare sensor/Zen acceptance under the selected explicit policy.
  • Real 1.18 login and request-handler semantics in the test target, plus duplicate hashes/full keys, late PATH/login replies, cancellation and expiry in each stage, failed sends and no automatic alteration of management routes.
  • Preserve the 55-second work cutoff, 60-second total, acknowledgement text and at most the intended emitting submissions per stage.

Hardware acceptance must compare captured packets and confirm the original 7188 case succeeds from an initially unregistered sensor. The additional successful Zen targets should be included without assuming how they learned Zen's identity. No diagnosis of those targets is complete until their actual packet exchange or client state is observed.
